title: Swachh Bharat: small actions for a clean India

summary.text: A family sweeps the house spotless and tips the dust outside the gate. Is the house clean now? In this lesson you sort one day of your own waste and find out what it is made of and where each part goes. You learn why wet and dry waste are kept apart, how a toilet and a compost pit make waste safe, and why spitting and littering harm people you never meet. You look at the Swachh Bharat Mission, at what it changed and what people still argue about, and at the workers who clean India every day.
summary.art: A doorstep swept clean with a small heap of dust and wrappers just outside the gate, a crow looking at the heap, and a child in the doorway looking at both.

intro.hook: Think of the last thing you threw away. Where is it right now, this minute? Who has touched it since it left your hand?
intro.text: Most of us cannot answer. The bin is where our knowing stops. But the thing did not stop. Someone lifted it, someone sorted it, and it is lying somewhere now, or it has become something else. Today you will be a detective of your own dustbin. You will find out what your family throws away in one day and follow each kind to where it goes next. Then you will see why a clean India is made of small actions, and what else it needs.
intro.art: A child's hand letting go of a banana peel and a chips packet over a bin, with two dotted paths leading out of the bin in different directions and ending in question marks.

outcomes: I can say what 'clean' means in science, and why a place can look clean and still be unsafe.
I can sort household waste into wet, dry and harmful, and say why mixing them spoils all three.
I can explain how wet waste turns into compost, and what happens to it in a dump with no air.
I can explain how germs from toilet waste and spit reach other people, and how toilets and habits stop them.
I can describe the Swachh Bharat Mission and give one thing it changed and one thing people still argue about.
I can name the people and other living beings who clean India, and say what the workers need to be safe.
I can choose three small actions for my home or street and say what each one changes.

explanations.concept: Clean means harmful things are kept away from mouths, water and soil. It is different from tidy
explanations.definition: In science, a clean place is one where germs and harmful waste cannot easily reach people, other living beings, water or food. A tidy place is one that looks neat.
explanations.description: A swept room looks clean. A glass of clear water looks clean. Looks can mislead. Germs are living beings too small to see, and some of them cause illness. One spoonful of clear water can hold more germs than there are people in a town. So scientists ask a different question from 'does it look neat?'. They ask whether anything harmful can travel from here to a mouth, to drinking water, to food or to the soil. A tidy lane with an open drain beside the hand pump is not clean. A muddy garden with a covered compost pit is.
examples: A shining white plate wiped with a dirty cloth carries more germs than before.
A forest floor is covered in fallen leaves and is not dirty. The leaves are food for the soil.
A neat row of plastic bottles on a beach is tidy, and the plastic is still in the wrong place.
Dust swept from a house onto the road has only moved.

perspectives.who: Doctors and public health scientists
perspectives.explanation: Clean means the paths that carry germs and poisons to bodies are blocked. It can be measured by counting germs in water or illness in a neighbourhood.

perspectives.who: Mary Douglas, a British anthropologist, in her 1966 book 'Purity and Danger'
perspectives.explanation: She wrote that dirt is 'matter out of place'. Soil in the garden is soil. The same soil on the bed is dirt. Every culture has its own rules about what belongs where, and calls the rule-breaking thing dirty.

perspectives.who: Thiruvalluvar, in Thirukkural, verse 298
perspectives.explanation: Outer cleanness comes from water. Inner cleanness shows in truthfulness. The verse holds that a person can be washed and still not clean, and it puts the two side by side.

explanations.art: Two pictures: a neat lane with an open drain running beside a hand pump, marked with a cross, and a leafy, muddy garden with a covered compost pit far from a covered water pot, marked with a tick.
explanations.context: This card says what 'clean' means in science and why looking neat is not the test.

explanations.concept: What is in India's dustbins: about half is food and plant waste
explanations.definition: Solid waste is everything solid that people throw away. Wet waste is the part that came from plants and animals and will rot. Dry waste is the part that will not rot quickly, such as paper, plastic, glass and metal.
explanations.description: India's towns and cities throw away about 1.6 lakh tonnes of solid waste every day. That is roughly a third of a kilogram for each town-dweller, each day. What is it made of? About half is wet waste: peels, leftover food, tea leaves, flowers, garden clippings. Wet waste rots, and rotting is useful in the right place. The rest is mostly dry waste: paper, cardboard, plastic, glass, metal and cloth. A small part is harmful waste, such as used bandages, nappies, batteries and old medicines. So most of what we call rubbish is either food for soil or material for a factory.
examples: A banana peel, an eggshell and used tea leaves are wet waste.
A milk packet, a newspaper and a steel-wool scrubber are dry waste.
A used plaster, a blade and a tube light are harmful waste.
A family of four in a town makes more than one kilogram of waste a day, which is about 500 kilograms in a year.
explanations.one_view: These amounts come from counts by India's Central Pollution Control Board and city surveys. The exact shares differ from town to town.
explanations.art: A large dustbin drawn as a bar split into three bands: a wide green band of peels and food, a blue band of paper, plastic, glass and metal, and a thin red band with a battery and a bandage.
explanations.context: This card gives the size and the make-up of India's waste, so the later cards on sorting make sense.

explanations.concept: Three bins: wet, dry and harmful. Mixing them spoils all three
explanations.definition: Segregation means keeping different kinds of waste apart from the moment they are thrown away.
explanations.description: Tip leftover sambar onto a newspaper. Now the paper is soggy and smelly, and no paper mill will take it. The sambar is full of ink and cannot go to compost. Two useful things have become one useless thing. That is why India's rules, made in 2016, ask every home to keep three kinds of waste apart. Wet waste goes in the green bin. Dry waste goes in the blue bin, rinsed and dry. Harmful waste, such as nappies, sanitary pads, bandages, blades and batteries, is wrapped and kept in a third bin. Sorting takes a few seconds at home. Un-mixing a truckload later is nearly impossible.
examples: A curd cup rinsed with a splash of water can be recycled. A curd cup with curd in it spoils the whole sack.
Broken glass and blades are wrapped in paper and marked, because a person will handle the bag.
Coconut shells and bones rot very slowly, so many towns ask for them in dry waste.
Old phones, chargers and bulbs are 'e-waste' and go to special collection points.

perspectives.who: Waste workers' groups, such as SWaCH in Pune and Hasiru Dala in Bengaluru
perspectives.explanation: Sorting at home is the single act that most changes a waste worker's day. Clean, dry material earns them money. Mixed waste cuts their hands and makes them ill.

perspectives.who: Some city engineers and companies
perspectives.explanation: People will never sort reliably, so cities should collect mixed waste and use machines to separate or burn it. Critics answer that machines sort wet Indian waste poorly and that burning it gives little energy and dirty smoke.

explanations.art: A green bin with peels, a blue bin with a rinsed bottle and folded paper, and a small red bin with a wrapped packet marked with a cross, and beside them one bin with everything mixed and dripping.
explanations.context: This card explains the three-bin rule and the reason for it.

explanations.concept: Wet waste becomes compost, with the help of countless small living beings
explanations.definition: Compost is the dark, crumbly, soil-like material left when living beings such as bacteria, fungi and earthworms have eaten and broken down plant and food waste, with air.
explanations.description: A peel left in a pot of soil does not vanish. Someone eats it. Bacteria and fungi, who are living beings mostly too small to see, feed on the peel. Earthworms, ants and beetles join in. They need three things: food, air and a little dampness. As they feed they give off warmth, and a big heap can get hotter inside than a summer afternoon. In two to three months the peels have become compost, dark and crumbly, smelling like earth after rain. Plants grow well in it. Nothing was thrown away. What the peel was made of went from a plant, to you, to the soil, and is ready for a plant again.
examples: A home composter can be a clay pot with holes, layered with dry leaves to let air in.
A heap that smells bad has too little air. Stirring it or adding dry leaves fixes this.
Cooked food, peels, tea leaves, flowers and eggshells can all be composted at home.
In Alappuzha, Kerala, neighbourhoods compost their wet waste in shared bins instead of sending it to a dump.

perspectives.who: Albert Howard and Gabrielle Howard, British plant scientists who worked in Indore from 1924 to 1931
perspectives.explanation: They studied how Indian farmers returned every scrap to the soil and worked out measured steps for it, known as the Indore method. Albert Howard wrote that the peasants of India were his professors. Gabrielle Howard, a trained plant scientist, did much of the research and is often left out.

perspectives.who: Soil scientists today
perspectives.explanation: Compost improves how soil holds water and feeds soil life. It carries less plant food than factory fertiliser, so many say that feeding the world needs both.

perspectives.who: Vrikshayurveda of Surapala, a Sanskrit book on plant care from about the 10th century CE
perspectives.explanation: It gives recipes for a liquid manure called kunapajala, made by letting animal and plant remains break down in water, and says which trees to feed with it. Turning waste into plant food is an old, written practice in India.

explanations.art: A cut-away clay pot composter in three layers: fresh peels on top, half-broken brown matter with earthworms in the middle, and dark crumbly compost at the bottom, with a magnified circle showing fungi threads and tiny bacteria.
explanations.context: This card explains what compost is and who makes it.

explanations.concept: The same peel in a dump, with no air, makes a gas that burns and warms the Earth
explanations.definition: Methane is a gas made when wet waste rots without air. It burns easily, and in the air it traps heat.
explanations.description: Now bury the same peel deep in a mountain of mixed rubbish. No air reaches it. Different bacteria take over, ones who live without air. They work slowly, and they give off a gas called methane. Methane has no smell and burns easily. Dumps catch fire from inside and smoulder for days. Methane that escapes also traps heat around the Earth, far more strongly than the same amount of the gas we breathe out. So one peel has two futures. With air, in a compost pot, the peel becomes soil in three months. Without air, in a dump, the peel becomes a fire risk and a warming gas.
examples: The Ghazipur dump in Delhi, begun in 1984, had grown to about 65 metres high by 2019. That is nearly as tall as the Qutub Minar.
Dark, bad-smelling liquid drains out of dumps and can seep into the water under the ground.
Some cities now trap dump gas in pipes and burn it for cooking or electricity.
A gobar gas plant on a farm uses the same airless rotting on purpose, in a closed tank, to make cooking gas from dung.
explanations.one_view: What rots with air and without air has been measured many times, and scientists agree on it.
explanations.art: One banana peel at the top with two arrows: one to a compost pot with a small plant growing, one to the inside of a huge rubbish mountain with bubbles of gas rising and a thin line of smoke.
explanations.context: This card shows why sending wet waste to a dump is harmful, by following one peel down two paths.

explanations.concept: Dry waste is recycled by people: India's waste pickers
explanations.definition: Recycling is turning used material into new things. A waste picker is a person who earns a living by collecting, sorting and selling used material.
explanations.description: A plastic bottle does not walk to a factory. In India, most recycling begins with a person. Waste pickers collect bottles, paper, metal and cardboard from bins, streets and dumps. They sort them by hand into dozens of kinds and sell them to dealers, who sell them to factories. Estimates of their number run from about 15 lakh to 40 lakh. Many are women, and many are Dalits. They save cities a great deal of money and keep mountains of material out of dumps. For years most had no gloves, no fixed pay and no thanks. Some have now formed their own groups and won identity cards and contracts.
examples: In Pune, the waste pickers' own cooperative, SWaCH, has collected sorted waste door to door for the city since 2008.
In Bengaluru, waste pickers were given city identity cards from 2011, after a campaign by the group Hasiru Dala.
A used drinks bottle can be shredded, melted and spun into thread for cloth.
A shiny chips packet is plastic and metal foil stuck together. It is very hard to recycle, so almost nobody buys it.

perspectives.who: Waste pickers' unions, such as the Kagad Kach Patra Kashtakari Panchayat in Pune, formed in 1993
perspectives.explanation: Waste picking is skilled work that serves the whole city and the environment. Pickers should be paid by the city, given safety gear and health care, and have first right to the dry waste.

perspectives.who: Some city planners
perspectives.explanation: Waste work by hand is unsafe and should be replaced by companies with trucks and machines. Pickers' groups answer that this takes away the living of the poorest workers and recycles less.

explanations.art: A woman in gloves and an apron at a sorting table with separate sacks for clear bottles, milk packets, cardboard, white paper and metal, and one small heap of shiny wrappers set aside.
explanations.context: This card shows that recycling in India depends on waste pickers, and what they ask for.

explanations.concept: Germs from toilet waste reach mouths by a few known paths
explanations.definition: Faeces is the solid waste a body passes out. Germs in faeces can reach another person's mouth through fingers, flies, fields, water and food.
explanations.description: Faeces, which many families call potty, carries very large numbers of germs. Most are harmless inside the gut, and some cause diarrhoea, cholera and typhoid. If faeces is left in the open, the germs travel. Fingers carry them. Flies land on the faeces and then on food. Rain washes them into wells and rivers. Feet carry them from fields. In 1958 two engineers, Edmund Wagner and Joseph Lanoix, drew all these paths in one picture for the World Health Organization. It shows where to block each path. A toilet blocks the first step. Washing hands with soap blocks fingers. Covering food blocks flies. Safe water blocks the rest.
examples: One fly can carry germs on the hairs of the legs from a heap to a plate in seconds.
A well downhill from an open field can be spoilt by one heavy shower.
Diarrhoea used to kill more than a lakh young children in India every year. The number has fallen as toilets, clean water and medicine spread.
A child's faeces carries as many germs as a grown-up's, so nappies need the same care.
explanations.one_view: These paths have been traced by many studies of outbreaks, and scientists agree on them.
explanations.art: A diagram with faeces on the left and a child's mouth on the right, joined by five arrows labelled fingers, flies, fields, water and food, with a toilet, soap, a food cover and a covered water pot each blocking an arrow.
explanations.context: This card explains how illness travels from toilet waste to people, which is the reason toilets and handwashing matter.

explanations.concept: How a twin-pit toilet makes waste safe without a sewer
explanations.definition: A twin-pit toilet is a toilet joined to two pits in the ground, used one at a time. In the resting pit, the waste slowly turns into safe, dry manure.
explanations.description: Most Indian villages have no sewer pipes. The twin-pit toilet was designed for them. The pan slopes steeply, so one mug of water flushes it. A bend in the pipe holds a little water, which keeps smell and flies from coming up. The pipe leads to one of two pits lined with bricks that have gaps between them. Water soaks away into the soil, and the soil filters it. When the first pit fills, after a few years, the pipe is turned to the second pit. The first is left to rest. In about a year or two, soil bacteria turn the contents into dry, crumbly manure with no smell and no harmful germs.
examples: A flush toilet with a tank uses about ten litres each time. A pour-flush pan needs about one and a half to two.
The pits are dug away from wells and hand pumps, so that soaked-away water is well filtered first.
Bindeshwar Pathak, who founded Sulabh in 1970, improved this design and spread it to lakhs of homes.
In cities, toilets drain to sewers and treatment plants, where bacteria in large tanks do the same cleaning work faster.

perspectives.who: Sanitation engineers
perspectives.explanation: The twin pit is cheap, saves water and needs no person to handle fresh waste. It suits most soils, though not places where the water under the ground is very near the surface.

perspectives.who: Diane Coffey and Dean Spears, researchers, in their 2017 book 'Where India Goes'
perspectives.explanation: In villages they surveyed, many families who owned a pit toilet did not use it. People feared the day the pit would need emptying, a job long forced on Dalits and seen as polluting. They argue that toilets alone do not end open defecation unless these beliefs change.

explanations.art: A cut-away side view of a toilet pan with a water-filled bend, a pipe leading to a Y-junction, one brick-lined pit in use with water soaking outward, and a second pit closed and marked 'resting'.
explanations.context: This card explains the design of the toilet most used in Swachh Bharat, and why owning one is not the same as using it.

explanations.concept: Covered drains and home toilets were built in the Harappan cities over 4,000 years ago
explanations.definition: The Harappan civilisation was a group of cities in the north-west of the Indian subcontinent, at its height from about 2600 BCE to 1900 BCE.
explanations.description: Planned sanitation in this land is very old. At Mohenjo-daro, Harappa, Lothal and Dholavira, from about 2600 BCE, many houses had a bathing floor of tightly fitted bricks. Some had a toilet. Waste water ran through a pipe in the wall into a drain along the street. The street drains were built of baked brick and covered with slabs. They sloped gently so that water kept moving. At some corners there were pits where solids settled and could be dug out. Few other cities in the world had anything like this at that time. Nobody knows who cleaned the drains, or how those workers were treated.
examples: Lothal, in Gujarat, had drains leading from houses to covered street drains and soak pits.
Dholavira, in Kutch, had large stone drains to carry storm water to its reservoirs.
Kautilya's Arthashastra, book 2, chapter 36, sets fines for throwing dirt on a road and for letting mud or water collect there, with higher fines on the king's road.
Rome's great sewer, the Cloaca Maxima, was begun about 600 BCE, some 2,000 years after the Harappan drains.

perspectives.who: Archaeologists such as Jonathan Mark Kenoyer
perspectives.explanation: The drains show shared rules and shared spending across a whole city. Someone planned the slopes, and someone kept the drains clear for centuries.

perspectives.who: Historians who ask about the workers
perspectives.explanation: The Harappan script has not been read, so we do not know if cleaning was shared by all, paid work, or forced on one group. Good drains tell us about engineering. They do not tell us whether the system was fair.

explanations.art: A Harappan street seen from above with brick houses, a small pipe from each house wall, and a brick drain along the street covered with stone slabs, one slab lifted to show water flowing.
explanations.context: This card shows that planned drains and toilets are an ancient achievement of this land, and says what we do not know about them.

explanations.concept: Spitting sends germs and stains into shared places
explanations.definition: Saliva is the liquid in the mouth. Sputum is the thicker liquid coughed up from the chest. Both can carry germs.
explanations.description: Spit looks like water. It carries whatever germs are living in a person's mouth, nose and chest. When someone with a chest illness coughs or spits, tiny drops fly into the air and can be breathed in by people nearby. Tuberculosis, called TB, spreads this way, mostly through coughing. India has more TB patients than any other country. Spit on a floor is also trodden through and touched by small children and by other animals. Spit mixed with paan or gutkha does one more thing. It is slightly acid and it stains. Red streaks on walls and stairs are hard to remove, and over years they can eat into steel.
examples: On Kolkata's Howrah Bridge, the steel bases of the hangers were found to be thinning from years of gutkha spit, and were given protective covers.
The railways spend a very large sum and a great deal of water every year washing spit stains from stations and coaches.
During the 2020 pandemic, spitting in public was made a punishable offence across India.
A person who needs to spit can use a wash basin, a toilet or a tissue that goes in a bin.

perspectives.who: Doctors who study tuberculosis
perspectives.explanation: TB spreads mainly through the air when a sick person coughs, and much less from spit on the ground. They support no-spitting rules for general hygiene, and say that finding and treating patients early prevents far more TB.

perspectives.who: The Buddhist monastic rules, in the Vinaya Pitaka, Sekhiya rules 74 and 75
perspectives.explanation: A monk or nun who is not ill is told not to pass waste or spit onto growing plants or into water. The rule is about 2,400 years old, and it protects water and crops that other beings depend on.

perspectives.who: Researchers who study habits
perspectives.explanation: Fines seldom work when nobody enforces them. People spit less where spittoons and basins are provided, where walls are clean to begin with, and where others around them do not spit.

explanations.art: A railway platform with a clean wall and a wash basin, a person bending to spit into the basin, and in a faded inset the same wall streaked red with a child's hand reaching towards it.
explanations.context: This card explains what is in spit, how it harms people and structures, and what helps people stop.

explanations.concept: Litter invites more litter, and one person's small act becomes everyone's problem
explanations.definition: Litter is waste left in a shared place. A shared place is one that belongs to everyone and so is easily cared for by no one.
explanations.description: Why does a person who would never throw a wrapper on the floor at home throw one on the road? One wrapper seems to make no difference. And a road is nobody's and everybody's. In 1990 the American researcher Robert Cialdini tested this. People found a paper slip on their car. In a car park already covered in litter, far more of them dropped the slip on the ground than in a clean car park. Litter tells the next person 'this is what people do here'. A clean street sends the opposite message. So the first wrapper matters most, and so does the first person who picks one up.
examples: A corner where one bag of rubbish is dumped at night often has ten bags by the weekend.
In 2008, researchers in the Netherlands found that people littered about twice as often in a lane with scribbled walls as in the same lane with clean walls.
In Mumbai's floods of 26 July 2005, plastic bags blocked storm drains and made the flooding worse.
Some towns paint rangoli or plant flowers on old dumping corners, and the dumping stops.

perspectives.who: Garrett Hardin, an American ecologist, in 1968
perspectives.explanation: He called this the 'tragedy of the commons'. Each person gains a little by misusing a shared thing, and the cost is spread over everyone. He believed only private ownership or strict government control could prevent ruin.

perspectives.who: Elinor Ostrom, an American scholar, who won the Nobel Prize in economics in 2009
perspectives.explanation: She studied forests, fisheries and water channels around the world, including in Nepal and India. She found many communities that cared for shared things very well for centuries, with their own rules, their own watchers and fair shares. The tragedy is not certain.

explanations.art: Two views of the same street corner: one clean with a single person holding a wrapper and looking for a bin, one already littered with the same person dropping the wrapper.
explanations.context: This card explains why people litter in shared places, with the experiments that tested it and two views on the cure.

explanations.concept: Street drains lead to rivers, and most of India's waste water reaches them untreated
explanations.definition: Sewage is the used water from toilets, kitchens and bathrooms. A sewage treatment plant cleans it before it is let into a river or the sea.
explanations.description: A wrapper dropped in a gutter does not stay there. The next rain carries it to a bigger drain, then to a stream, then to a river and at last to the sea. The used water from homes takes the same road. In a treatment plant, bacteria in large tanks eat most of the waste in the water before it is let go. India's towns and cities make about 72,000 million litres of sewage a day. Less than one-third of it is treated. The rest flows into rivers and lakes as it is. People downstream bathe in that river, water crops with it and often drink from it. So do fish, birds and dolphins.
examples: The Ganga passes about a hundred towns and cities, each adding waste water to what the last one sent down.
The Namami Gange programme, begun in 2014, builds treatment plants and stops drains from emptying straight into the river.
Flowers offered at temples are now collected in several cities and turned into compost and incense sticks, instead of going into the river.
The Ganga river dolphin, India's national water animal, is nearly blind and finds fish by sound. Dirty, noisy water makes this harder for them.

perspectives.who: River engineers
perspectives.explanation: A river is a flow of water to be measured and managed. The cure is more treatment plants, enough clean flow kept in the river, and factories made to treat their own waste.

perspectives.who: The Uttarakhand High Court, in March 2017
perspectives.explanation: The court declared the Ganga and the Yamuna to be living persons in law, with rights of their own. The Supreme Court put this order on hold a few months later, because it raised hard questions, such as who answers if a river floods.

perspectives.who: The Māori people of the Whanganui River in New Zealand
perspectives.explanation: They say: 'I am the river, and the river is me.' In March 2017 New Zealand's parliament recognised the Whanganui as a legal person, with two guardians to speak for the river.

perspectives.who: The Atharva Veda, book 12, hymn 1, verse 35
perspectives.explanation: The poet tells the Earth: whatever I dig from you, may it quickly grow again. May I not pierce your vital parts or your heart. The hymn treats the Earth as someone who can be hurt.

explanations.art: A side view following water from a house drain to a street gutter with a floating wrapper, to a stream, to a wide river with a dolphin and a bathing ghat, to the sea.
explanations.context: This card follows waste water from the home to the river, and asks whether a river is a thing or a someone.

explanations.concept: The Swachh Bharat Mission: toilets for every home, and cleaner towns
explanations.definition: The Swachh Bharat Mission is a programme of the Government of India, begun on 2 October 2014, to end defecation in the open and to manage waste in every village and town.
explanations.description: On 2 October 2014, Mahatma Gandhi's birthday, the Government of India began the Swachh Bharat Mission. 'Swachh Bharat' means 'Clean India'. Its first aim was that nobody should have to defecate in the open by 2 October 2019. The government gave families money to build toilets, and reports that more than ten crore home toilets were built in villages. Its second aim is clean towns: door-to-door collection, sorted waste, and no more rubbish mountains. Each year a survey ranks cities on cleanliness. It was not India's first such programme. Earlier ones began in 1986 and 1999. This one was far larger, and it made cleanliness something the whole country talked about.
examples: The mission's sign is Gandhi's round spectacles, with 'Swachh' on one lens and 'Bharat' on the other.
A village where nobody defecates in the open is called 'open defecation free', or ODF.
The second stage, begun in 2020 and 2021, adds compost pits, soak pits, plastic collection and treating waste water.
Public toilets were built at bus stands, markets and petrol pumps.
explanations.one_view: These are the stated aims and dates of the programme. What it achieved is argued over, and that argument is in the next card.
explanations.art: A village lane with small new toilets beside each house, a painted wall showing Gandhi's round spectacles, and a woman with a mug walking to her toilet door.
explanations.context: This card says what the Swachh Bharat Mission is, when it began and what it set out to do.

explanations.concept: Did Swachh Bharat work? The counts disagree
explanations.definition: To judge a programme, people compare what was measured before and after. Different ways of measuring can give different answers.
explanations.description: In October 2019 the government declared rural India open defecation free. It had counted toilets, village by village. Independent researchers counted something else: what people actually do. In 2018 a team revisited villages in Bihar, Madhya Pradesh, Rajasthan and Uttar Pradesh. Open defecation there had fallen a great deal, from about 70 in every 100 people to about 44. That is a big change in four years, and it is not zero. About one in four people who owned a toilet still went in the open. A national health survey in 2019 to 2021 found about one household in five without a toilet in use. So both things are true. Very much changed, and the work is unfinished.
examples: A toilet with no water nearby, or with a pit the family fears to empty, often becomes a store room.
A 2024 study linked the mission to tens of thousands fewer deaths of babies each year.
Some reports described officials shaming or fining people to push up the numbers.
Women and girls gain most from a home toilet: safety at night, and no long wait for darkness.

perspectives.who: The Government of India
perspectives.explanation: More than ten crore toilets were built and every village declared itself open defecation free, checked by a national survey. Toilet coverage rose from under 40 in 100 homes to nearly all in five years.

perspectives.who: Aashish Gupta, Diane Coffey, Dean Spears and colleagues at the research group r.i.c.e., in 2018 and 2019
perspectives.explanation: Their repeat survey found a large fall in open defecation, and also that it remained common in the four states they studied. They found some pressure and threats used on poor families, and argued that counting toilets overstates success.

perspectives.who: Suman Chakrabarti and colleagues, in 2024
perspectives.explanation: Comparing districts over twenty years, they found that districts where many toilets were built under the mission had clearly fewer deaths of babies and young children. They estimated 60,000 to 70,000 fewer infant deaths a year.

explanations.art: A balance with two pans: on one, a tall stack of small toilet models with a tick, and on the other a clipboard with a tally of people, some ticked and some not.
explanations.context: This card gives the evidence on both sides of a real argument about how much the mission achieved.

explanations.concept: Who cleans India? Sanitation workers, an old injustice, and two views of it
explanations.definition: A sanitation worker is a person whose job is to clean streets, drains, toilets, sewers or septic tanks. Manual scavenging means cleaning human waste by hand.
explanations.description: Every clean street was cleaned by someone. Every sewer was unblocked by someone. In India, for many centuries, this work was forced on certain castes, the people now called Dalits, and their children were given no other choice. Cleaning human waste by hand was banned by law in 1993 and again in 2013. It still happens. Workers still go down into sewers and septic tanks without safety gear, and by the government's own count more than 300 died doing so in five recent years. A clean India has to mean safe machines, fair pay and respect for these workers. It also means the work is no longer tied to birth.
examples: Bezwada Wilson, born into a family of manual scavengers in Karnataka, leads the Safai Karmachari Andolan and won the Ramon Magsaysay Award in 2016.
In 2018 engineers in Kerala built 'Bandicoot', a robot that goes down a manhole and clears blocked sewers, so that no person has to.
In Kerala, women of the Haritha Karma Sena collect sorted waste from homes as paid, uniformed workers.
Wrapping a blade and rinsing a bottle are small acts that protect a worker's hands.

perspectives.who: Mahatma Gandhi
perspectives.explanation: He cleaned toilets himself, at his ashrams and at the 1901 Congress meeting in Calcutta, and asked every person to clean up their own waste. He called the work noble, like a mother's care, and wanted all castes to share it.

perspectives.who: B. R. Ambedkar, in his 1945 book 'What Congress and Gandhi Have Done to the Untouchables'
perspectives.explanation: He wrote that in India a person is a scavenger because of birth and not because of the work. Calling the work noble, he argued, keeps the same people doing it. What is needed is an end to caste, and other work, schooling and equal rights for those families.

perspectives.who: Bezwada Wilson and the Safai Karmachari Andolan
perspectives.explanation: Building crores of toilets without sewers or machines means more pits and tanks for people to clean by hand. They ask that the money and attention given to toilets also go to ending manual scavenging.

explanations.art: A sanitation worker in a helmet, gloves and boots operating a robot arm that reaches down an open manhole, with a cleared drain running behind.
explanations.context: This card names the people who do India's cleaning, tells the truth about caste and danger in that work, and gives Gandhi's and Ambedkar's differing views.

explanations.concept: Places that did it: Indore, Ambikapur, Alappuzha and Mawlynnong
explanations.definition: A zero-landfill place is one where almost nothing is sent to a dump, because wet waste is composted or turned to gas and dry waste is sold for recycling.
explanations.description: Four places in India show that it can be done, each in a different way. Indore, in Madhya Pradesh, has been ranked India's cleanest city every year from 2017 to 2023. Every home hands over sorted waste to a truck each morning. A plant turns the city's wet waste into gas that runs its buses. Ambikapur, in Chhattisgarh, is cleaned by women's groups who sort waste into many kinds and sell it. Alappuzha, in Kerala, closed its dump and composts in each neighbourhood. Mawlynnong, a Khasi village in Meghalaya, has had bamboo dustbins on every path for years, and every family sweeps the lanes.
examples: Indore's gas plant, opened in 2022, takes about 550 tonnes of wet waste a day.
Ambikapur opened a 'Garbage Café' in 2019, where a kilogram of plastic waste buys a full meal.
In 2017 the United Nations Environment Programme named Alappuzha among five cities in the world tackling waste well.
A travel magazine called Mawlynnong the cleanest village in Asia in 2003.

perspectives.who: City officials in Indore
perspectives.explanation: Success came from strict rules: daily collection from every door, fines for littering and mixing, and thousands of workers and vehicles paid for by a user fee.

perspectives.who: People's groups in Alappuzha and Mawlynnong
perspectives.explanation: Success came from neighbours agreeing among themselves, with little machinery and little cost. They say a big city's plants and trucks are costly to run and that small, local ways last longer.

explanations.art: A map of India with four pins and small pictures: a collection truck with separate compartments in Indore, women at a sorting shed in Ambikapur, a row of compost bins in Alappuzha, and a cone-shaped bamboo dustbin on a village path in Mawlynnong.
explanations.context: This card gives four real Indian examples of clean places and shows there is more than one way to get there.

explanations.concept: Other living beings clean India too, and losing them costs lives
explanations.definition: A scavenger is an animal who eats dead animals or leftover food. Scavengers and decomposers together clear away what would otherwise pile up and rot.
explanations.description: Long before any mission, India had cleaners. Vultures stripped a dead cow to the bones in under an hour. Crows, kites, ants, dung beetles and bacteria took what was left. In the 1990s India's vultures began to die. The scientist Vibhu Prakash, of the Bombay Natural History Society, recorded the crash. More than 95 in every 100 were lost in about fifteen years. In 2004 a team led by Lindsay Oaks found the cause. A pain medicine given to cattle, called diclofenac, poisoned vultures who ate the dead cattle. With the vultures gone, carcasses lay rotting, stray dogs grew in number, and rabies spread. India banned the medicine for animals in 2006.
examples: A 2024 study estimated that the loss of vultures led to about one lakh extra human deaths a year in India between 2000 and 2005.
Black kites circle above markets and dumps in most Indian cities and pick up scraps.
Ants clear a dropped crumb of food from a floor within hours.
Vulture breeding centres at Pinjore in Haryana and elsewhere are now raising and releasing young vultures.

perspectives.who: Ecologists
perspectives.explanation: Scavengers do public health work for free. The vulture crash is one of the clearest cases anywhere of people's health depending on another animal.

perspectives.who: The Parsi community of India
perspectives.explanation: For centuries Parsis have laid their dead in open towers for vultures, so that the body neither dirties the earth nor wastes fire. With vultures gone, the community has had to rethink an ancient practice.

explanations.art: A sky with circling vultures and kites above a field, a crow and a line of ants on the ground, and in a faded inset the same field with no birds, a carcass and several stray dogs.
explanations.context: This card shows that other animals do much of India's cleaning, and what happened when vultures were lost.

explanations.concept: The cleanest waste is the waste never made: refuse and reuse come before recycle
explanations.definition: To refuse is to not take a thing you do not need. To reuse is to use a thing again as it is. Both come before recycling, which needs energy, water and work.
explanations.description: Sorting helps. Making less helps more. Every wrapper not taken is one that nobody has to collect, sort or bury. India has old habits that do this. Food is served on a banana leaf or a plate of stitched sal leaves, and the plate goes to a cow or the compost heap. Tea comes in a clay kulhad. Lunch travels in a steel tiffin for thirty years. Milk came in a returned bottle. On 1 July 2022 India banned a list of throw-away plastic items, such as straws, plastic cutlery and thin carry bags. People disagree on how well bans work, and on what should replace plastic.
examples: A steel bottle refilled every day for a year replaces hundreds of plastic bottles.
At many weddings and temple feasts in South India, meals are still served on banana leaves.
A cloth bag kept by the door only helps if it goes to the market every time.
Mending a strap, a zip or a chappal keeps a whole thing out of the bin.

perspectives.who: Zero-waste campaigners, such as Bea Johnson, and the makers of India's 2022 ban
perspectives.explanation: Recycling cannot keep up with what is made. The only sure answer is to stop making throw-away things and to bring back refill and reuse.

perspectives.who: Researchers who measure a product's whole life, such as a Danish government study in 2018
perspectives.explanation: A cotton or paper bag takes more water, land and energy to make than a thin plastic one. It is better only if it is used a great many times. Swapping plastic for another throw-away thing can make matters worse.

perspectives.who: Street vendors and small shopkeepers
perspectives.explanation: Plastic is cheap, light and keeps food dry. Leaf plates and paper cost more and leak. They ask that affordable replacements come before fines.

explanations.art: A banana leaf with a meal, a clay kulhad of tea, a steel tiffin and a cloth bag on one side, and on the other a pile of plastic plates, cups, spoons and bags.
explanations.context: This card explains why making less waste beats recycling, shows Indian ways of doing it, and gives the argument about bans.

explanations.concept: Small actions and big systems: a clean-up helps, and it is not enough alone
explanations.definition: A small action is something one person or family can do. A system is the set of rules, services and designs that shape what everyone does.
explanations.description: In October 2015 a lawyer named Afroz Shah and his 84-year-old neighbour began picking rubbish off Versova beach in Mumbai. People joined them, weekend after weekend. In under two years, volunteers removed more than 50 lakh kilograms of waste. In 2018 olive ridley turtle hatchlings were seen on Versova for the first time in about twenty years. That is what small actions can do. But the sea brought new plastic with every tide, because factories kept making it and drains kept carrying it. So a clean India needs both. People must carry their wrapper to a bin, sort, compost and not spit. Cities must collect, and companies must make less throw-away packing.
examples: Small actions a child can take: keep a wrapper in your pocket until you find a bin, rinse and sort, and carry your own bottle.
A street that sweeps together once a month also learns who its neighbours are.
Counting litter by brand name during a clean-up shows which companies' packing ends up on the ground.
India's rules now require companies to collect back as much plastic packing as they sell.

perspectives.who: Afroz Shah and other clean-up leaders
perspectives.explanation: Picking up waste with your own hands changes how you see it. People who have cleaned a beach stop littering and start asking their city and their shops for change.

perspectives.who: Groups such as Break Free From Plastic, and researchers on plastic pollution
perspectives.explanation: Clean-ups treat the result and leave the cause. For decades, packaging companies paid for anti-litter campaigns that blamed the public while they made more throw-away packing. Real change comes from rules on what is made.

perspectives.who: Researchers who study habits, such as Robert Cialdini
perspectives.explanation: Both matter, because each feeds the other. People follow what they see others doing, and governments act when enough people care.

explanations.art: A beach with a line of volunteers of all ages passing buckets of rubbish hand to hand, a tiny turtle hatchling crawling to the sea, and a drain pipe at the edge still carrying wrappers onto the sand.
explanations.context: This card shows what small actions achieved on one Mumbai beach, and gives the argument about whether individuals or systems matter more.

agreed.text: Where people gain toilets, clean water and handwashing, fewer children fall ill and more grow to their full height.
agreed.evidence: Studies across India and other countries, including work by Dean Spears published in 2013, found that children in places with more open defecation were shorter on average for their age, because repeated gut infections stop the body from using food well.

agreed.text: Cholera and typhoid spread through water and food dirtied by faeces, and not through bad smells.
agreed.evidence: John Snow mapped cholera deaths around one water pump in London in 1854. In Calcutta in 1884, Robert Koch identified the cholera bacteria, and in 1959 Sambhu Nath De showed how their poison causes the illness.

agreed.text: Plastic in the sea breaks into smaller and smaller pieces and does not go away.
agreed.evidence: Since Richard Thompson's team named 'microplastics' in 2004, they have been found in sea salt, in fish, in rain and in human blood. Their effect on health is still being studied.

agreed.text: Burning rubbish in the open makes harmful smoke.
agreed.evidence: Measurements of the air beside burning waste find fine particles and poisonous gases, especially when plastic burns. Indian law bans open burning of waste.

challenging.claim: Rural India became open defecation free in 2019.
challenging.for: Records show more than ten crore toilets built, and every village declared itself open defecation free, backed by a national survey of toilet use.
challenging.against: The r.i.c.e. survey of 2018 and the National Family Health Survey of 2019 to 2021 both found a real share of people still without a toilet in use. Counting toilets is easier than counting habits.
challenging.context: A claim made with great confidence and questioned with careful surveys. Both sides agree that open defecation fell sharply.

challenging.claim: Burning waste to make electricity is the answer to India's rubbish mountains.
challenging.who: Some city governments and waste-to-energy companies
challenging.for: Burning shrinks waste to a small amount of ash, needs little land and makes some electricity. Countries such as Japan and Sweden burn much of their waste.
challenging.against: Indian waste is about half wet, so it burns poorly. Several Indian plants have shut or been fined for dirty smoke. Burning also destroys the paper and plastic that waste pickers earn from.
challenging.context: A solution used widely abroad that has struggled in India. It shows why the make-up of waste matters.

challenging.claim: A river should have the rights of a person.
challenging.who: The Uttarakhand High Court in 2017, the Māori of the Whanganui River, and many environmental lawyers
challenging.for: A river with rights can be defended in court by guardians, as a child can. It matches how many peoples have long thought of rivers.
challenging.against: India's Supreme Court put the order on hold. Critics ask who pays when a river with legal personhood floods a town, and say strong pollution laws, properly enforced, would do more.
challenging.context: A new legal idea with old roots. It is here because it changes what 'keeping a river clean' means.

challenging.claim: Litter is caused by careless people, so teaching the public is the cure.
challenging.who: Anti-litter campaigns in many countries since the 1950s
challenging.for: Experiments show that reminders, clean surroundings and good examples do reduce littering.
challenging.against: Historians such as Finis Dunaway have shown that packaging companies funded many of these campaigns to turn attention away from throw-away packing itself. Where there are no bins and no collection, careful people have nowhere to put waste.
challenging.context: The usual view of litter, challenged by people who ask who gains from blaming the public. Most researchers now say both behaviour and packaging matter.

big_questions.q: Soil in a garden is soil, and the same soil on a bed is dirt. So is 'dirty' something in the thing, or something about where the thing is?
big_questions.hint: Try it with a banana peel, a fallen leaf and a drop of water in three different places.

big_questions.q: A peel turns to soil, and the soil grows a plant. At what moment does the peel stop being waste?
big_questions.hint: Think about who is eating the peel at each stage.

big_questions.q: If you sweep your house clean and push the dust onto the road, have you made the world cleaner, dirtier or the same?
big_questions.hint: Ask where the edge of 'your place' really is, and who drew it.

big_questions.q: A forest has no dustbins and no sweepers, and is not buried in waste. What does a forest do that a city does not?
big_questions.hint: Follow a fallen leaf in a forest and a wrapper in a city, step by step.

big_questions.q: Is it fair that the people who make the least waste often do the most cleaning? What would a fair way look like?
big_questions.hint: Think about who cleans in your home, your school and your street.

big_questions.q: A government counts toilets built. Researchers count toilets used. Which count tells you more, and why might the two differ?
big_questions.hint: Think of something in your home that is owned and not used.

big_questions.q: Can a river be a person? What would the Ganga ask for, if a guardian could speak for her?
big_questions.hint: List what a river needs to stay a river.

big_questions.q: Nobody saw you drop it, and nobody will know. Is there still a reason not to litter?
big_questions.hint: Think about who meets the wrapper next, and what the next passer-by learns from seeing it.

big_questions.q: Who should do more for a clean India: each person, the city or the companies that make the packing?
big_questions.hint: Try taking away each one in turn, and see what stops working.

story.title: Mariyamma's Table
story.note: A made-up story set in Bengaluru. Sahana, her father and Mariyamma are imagined. What is real: Bengaluru has dry waste collection centres where waste pickers sort material into many kinds, waste pickers there have held city identity cards since 2011, clear drinks bottles are recycled into polyester thread, shiny multi-layer wrappers have almost no buyers, and mixed waste injures the people who sort it.
text: Sahana's teacher had given the class a strange task. 'Choose one thing you throw away this week,' she said. 'Find out where it goes.'

Sahana, who was eight, chose two things, because she could not decide. A juice bottle and a chips packet. On Saturday morning she and her father, Prakash, walked behind the collection auto to a shed at the end of the main road. A board said 'Dry Waste Collection Centre'.

Inside, a woman in a green apron stood at a long table. Sacks hung open all around her like the pockets of a huge coat. Her hands moved faster than Sahana could follow. A bottle flew into one sack. A milk packet into another. A flattened carton into a third.
'Mariyamma,' said Sahana's father, 'my daughter has homework. She wants to see where our garbage goes.'
Mariyamma did not stop. 'I do not have any garbage here,' she said. 'Come and look.'

She held up a clear bottle. 'This is PET. It goes to a factory that cuts it into flakes and spins the flakes into thread. In a few months somebody will wear it as a shirt.' She held up a milk packet. 'This is a different plastic, soft. It becomes pipes and sheets.' She tapped the cartons, the white paper, the newspapers, the tins. 'Each one has a buyer. Each one has a name. Twenty-eight kinds on this table. You call all of it garbage because you have finished with it. I have only begun.'
Sahana found her juice bottle in the pile. She knew it by the torn label. Mariyamma took it, twisted off the cap, dropped the cap in one sack and the bottle in another. 'Shirt,' she said.
'And this?' Sahana held out the chips packet.

Mariyamma turned it over. It was shiny silver inside and bright red outside. 'This one is two things stuck together, plastic and metal, so thin that nobody can pull them apart. No factory wants it. I pick up hundreds of these every day and nobody pays me one rupee for them.' She dropped it into a bin by itself. 'It will be burnt in a cement factory, or it will sit in a dump longer than you will live.'
Sahana looked at the packet in the bin. It had held chips for about ten minutes.
The auto tipped out a new load. One bag split open, and Sahana smelt it before she saw it. Rice and sambar, soaked into newspapers, wrapped round a broken tube light.

Mariyamma's hands stopped for the first time. She pulled on a second pair of gloves. 'This bag is from a house that does not sort,' she said. 'The paper is ruined. The food is ruined. And the glass is waiting for my fingers.' She showed Sahana a pale scar across her palm.
Sahana's father shifted his feet. 'We pay the collection fee every month,' he said. 'Is sorting not the centre's job?'

'Sorting is my job, sir,' said Mariyamma. 'I am good at it. But it is your waste. When a bag comes rinsed and dry, it is like a letter from that house. It says: I know a person will open this. When a bag comes like this one...' She lifted the dripping paper. 'This letter says: I do not know you are there.'
Outside, a crow was pulling a piece of roti from the gutter. A cow nosed at a plastic bag for the peels inside.

'For years the police chased us from the bins as thieves,' Mariyamma said. She touched the card pinned to her apron. It had her photo and the city's stamp. 'Now this says I work for the city. I would like gloves that last, and a pension. But I will tell you what I would like most.' She looked at Sahana. 'I would like that packet not to be made.'
On the way home Sahana was quiet. At the gate she stopped. 'Appa, when does a thing become garbage?'
Her father thought about it. 'When we throw it, I suppose.'

'No,' said Sahana slowly. 'The bottle is not garbage. Mariyamma has a name for it. The peel is not garbage to the cow. I think a thing is only garbage when nobody anywhere knows what to do with it next.' She frowned. 'Like the chips packet. So who made it garbage? Me, or the people who made the packet?'
Her father opened his mouth, and found that he did not know.
story.epiphany: Mariyamma has a name and a buyer for almost everything on her table. A thing becomes waste only when nobody knows its next use, and that is decided partly at home and partly where the thing is designed.
ask: Mariyamma said 'I do not have any garbage here.' What did she mean?
She called a sorted bag 'a letter' from a house. What does your family's bag say?
Sahana's father said sorting is the centre's job because he pays a fee. Mariyamma said it is his waste. Who do you agree with, and why?
Who made the chips packet into garbage: Sahana, the company, or someone else?
art: A shed with a long table, a woman in a green apron and gloves sorting swiftly, and open sacks hanging all around her.
A girl holding out a shiny red chips packet to the woman, who holds a clear bottle in her other hand.

how_we_found_out.story: For centuries, people in many countries believed that illness came from bad air. The idea was called miasma. It fitted what they saw: the smelliest, dirtiest lanes had the most sickness. In 1854 cholera struck Soho, in London. A doctor named John Snow marked every death on a street map. The marks crowded round one water pump in Broad Street. Workers at a nearby brewery, who drank beer and not pump water, stayed well. Snow had the pump handle taken off. The leaders of the city did not accept his idea for years. In the same year, in Florence, Filippo Pacini saw the cholera germ under his microscope, and was ignored. In 1884, in Calcutta, Robert Koch found the same germ in a water tank used by sick families, and the idea of bad air began to give way. In 1959, also in Calcutta, Sambhu Nath De showed how the germ's poison makes the gut pour out water. His work led to the simple salt-and-sugar drink that now saves lakhs of lives. He was never given a major prize.
how_we_found_out.who: John Snow, Filippo Pacini, Robert Koch, Sambhu Nath De
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: People believed that bad smells themselves caused disease. It was believable because dirty, smelly places really did have more illness. Snow's map and the later finding of the germ showed that the cause was in the water, carried from human waste.

roots.context: You have followed your family's waste out of the door and seen where it goes. Now we ask where 'my place' ends, and what that tells us about ourselves and the world.

deep_truth.truth: You sorted one day of your family's waste and asked where each thing goes next. Every single thing went to a place where somebody lives: a sorter's hands, a cow's mouth, a drain, a river. A fly from the heap at the corner can land on your plate. So one home cannot be clean alone. Clean is something a whole place does together.
deep_truth.habit: We speak of 'my house' and 'outside' as two separate places, and feel that pushing dirt over the line makes it gone. That line is drawn by us. Germs, water, flies and wrappers cross it without noticing.
deep_truth.evidence: In the dustbin count, not one item ended at the bin. Each had a next place and a next someone. The paths of germs from open waste to a mouth, by fingers, flies, fields, water and food, all cross from 'outside' to 'inside'.

three.who_am_i: Your body takes in food and water and gives back peels, breath, sweat and waste every day. What leaves you becomes part of soil, water and other bodies. So you are less a closed box and more a place that things pass through. Knowing this, you can ask where 'you' end.
three.what_is_life: In a forest, one being's waste is always another being's food. A leaf feeds a fungus, a fungus feeds a beetle, a beetle feeds a bird. Life keeps going by passing things on. Composting a peel puts you back inside that passing-on.
three.what_is_this_world: The Earth has no outside bin. Everything ever thrown away is still here, changed or unchanged. A world where nothing can leave is a world where everything is shared, whether we mean to share it or not.

roots.thread: The lesson began with a house swept clean and dust outside the gate. It ends with the gate looking less like a border. The water in your tap passed through other homes upstream. The person who sorts your bag is touched by what you put in it. The crow, the cow and the river meet your waste before any machine does. Seeing these links plainly is the science of public health. It also points further. Consciousness is the ground from which the house, the street and the river all arise, and none of them stands apart. Many people do not accept this last step, and one strong objection is given below.

teachings.teaching: Outer cleanness is made by water. Inner cleanness is seen in truthfulness.
teachings.link: The lesson shows how water, soap and toilets make the outside clean. The verse adds that a person can do all this and still deceive. Telling ourselves the dust is 'gone' when it is only outside the gate is a small untruth of this kind.

teachings.source: Atharva Veda, book 12, hymn 1 (the Hymn to the Earth), verse 35
teachings.teaching: Whatever I dig from you, O Earth, may it quickly grow again. May I not pierce your vital parts or your heart.
teachings.link: The poet takes from the Earth and promises not to harm her. The lesson's science shows what that takes: returning wet waste to soil and keeping poisons out of water. The hymn speaks to the Earth as a someone. Science describes the Earth's soils and waters, and has no test for whether the Earth is a someone.

teachings.source: The saying of the Whanganui Māori people of New Zealand, written into their country's law in 2017
teachings.teaching: 'I am the river, and the river is me.'
teachings.link: The water in a child's body was river and rain not long ago, and will be again. That is measured science. The Māori saying takes it as a statement of who they are.

science.text: The atoms in a peel, in soil, in a plant and in a child are the same atoms passed around. Matter is never used up. It only moves and changes form.
Whether rivers, forests or the Earth as a whole can be said to have awareness is a question a few scientists and philosophers take seriously and most do not.

other_view.view: Ambedkar warned that fine words about unity and the nobility of cleaning have long been used while one group of people was made to do all the dirty work. On his view, what matters is not a feeling of oneness. What matters is law, schooling, machines and equal rights, so that no person is born into cleaning up after others.

practice.title: Follow one thing
practice.say: Give your child one thing from today's waste, such as a peel or a clean wrapper. Say: 'Hold this in your hand. Take three slow breaths. Now, with your eyes closed, go backwards. Where was this before it reached our home? Who touched it? Go as far back as you can.' Wait. Then say: 'Now go forwards. Where will it be tomorrow? In a month? In a hundred years? Who will meet it?' Then let your child put it in the right bin.
practice.kid: Take one thing you are about to throw away. Hold it and take three slow breaths. Close your eyes. Think backwards: where was it before your home, and who touched it? Then think forwards: where will it be tomorrow, in a month, in a hundred years? Who will meet it? Now put it in the right bin.

ask: Where does your home end? At the door, the gate, the drain or the river?
In a forest nothing is waste. What would have to change for that to be true in your home?
If the person who sorts your waste could send your family one message, what do you think it would be?
Is the Earth a thing we live on, or someone we live with? How would you decide?
roots.art: A child sitting with eyes closed, holding a banana peel in cupped hands, with a faint circle behind showing a banana plant, a market, a compost pot and a new seedling joined by arrows.

open_questions.q: What do tiny pieces of plastic do inside living bodies?
open_questions.why_open: Microplastics have been found in fish, in birds and in human blood. Studies on health effects are new and small, and scientists cannot yet say how much harm they cause.

open_questions.q: What makes a whole village or city change a habit and keep the change?
open_questions.why_open: Indore and Mawlynnong changed in very different ways. Researchers have ideas about rules, examples and pride, and cannot yet predict which places will hold their gains.

open_questions.q: How many people in India still defecate in the open?
open_questions.why_open: Government records and independent surveys give different numbers, because they count different things, and asking people about a private habit is hard to do accurately.

open_questions.q: Can any living being eat plastic fast enough to matter?
open_questions.why_open: In 2016 Japanese scientists found bacteria who slowly digest one kind of bottle plastic. Whether such bacteria or their enzymes can ever clear real waste at useful speed is not known.

open_questions.q: Should rivers, forests and animals have rights in law?
open_questions.why_open: Courts in India, New Zealand, Ecuador and Colombia have answered in different ways. It is a question of values as well as science, and countries are still working it out.

terms.meaning: Free of harmful things, so that nothing dangerous can reach a mouth, water, food or soil.
terms.example: A hand pump with a covered drain around it is clean, even if the ground is muddy.
terms.art: A hand pump with a concrete platform, a covered drain and a girl filling a steel pot.

terms.meaning: Neat and in order, whether or not the place is safe.
terms.example: A shelf of bottles in a straight row is tidy. The shelf can still be dusty.
terms.art: A shelf of plastic bottles lined up exactly, with dust visible on the shelf edge.

terms.meaning: Living beings so small that you need a microscope to see them. Some make people ill and most do not.
terms.example: Germs ride on unwashed fingers from a toilet door handle to a roti.
terms.art: A fingertip drawn very large with tiny round and rod-shaped germs on it.

terms.meaning: Everything solid that people throw away.
terms.example: Peels, wrappers, broken pots and old shoes are all solid waste.
terms.art: A heap of peels, wrappers, a broken pot and a worn chappal on newspaper.

terms.meaning: Waste that came from plants and animals and will rot.
terms.example: A banana peel, tea leaves and leftover rice are wet waste.
terms.art: A banana peel, used tea leaves and a bowl of leftover rice in a green bin.

terms.meaning: Waste that does not rot quickly, such as paper, plastic, glass, metal and cloth.
terms.example: A newspaper, a rinsed milk packet and an empty tin are dry waste.
terms.art: A newspaper, a milk packet and a tin lying in a blue bin.

terms.meaning: Waste that can hurt the people who handle it or poison water and soil.
terms.example: A used bandage, a battery and a broken tube light are harmful waste.
terms.art: A wrapped bandage, a battery and a tube light in a small bag marked with a red cross.

terms.meaning: Old electrical things such as phones, chargers, bulbs and batteries. They hold metals that can be reused and poisons that must be kept out of soil.
terms.example: A broken phone charger goes to an e-waste collection point and not to the dustbin.
terms.art: A tangle of old chargers and a dead phone in a cardboard box at a collection point.

terms.meaning: Keeping different kinds of waste apart from the moment they are thrown away.
terms.example: Putting a peel in one bin and a clean paper in another is segregation.
terms.art: Two hands dropping a peel into a green bin and a clean paper into a blue bin.

terms.meaning: Dark, crumbly, soil-like stuff made when tiny living beings eat plant and food waste.
terms.example: Peels left in a pot with dry leaves become compost in two to three months.
terms.art: A hand holding a scoop of dark crumbly compost above a clay pot with a seedling.

terms.meaning: Tiny living beings, each made of one cell, found in soil, water, air and our bodies. Most are harmless and many do useful work.
terms.example: Bacteria in soil eat a peel and turn the peel into compost.
terms.art: A peel with tiny rod-shaped bacteria drawn very large on the peel's surface.

terms.meaning: Living beings such as mushrooms and moulds. They feed on dead plants and animals and break them down.
terms.example: The white fuzz on an old chapati is a fungus feeding on the chapati.
terms.art: A stale chapati with white fuzzy threads and a small mushroom beside the chapati.

terms.meaning: A gas made when wet waste rots without air. It burns easily and it traps heat around the Earth.
terms.example: A cow-dung gas plant makes methane on purpose and burns the gas for cooking.
terms.art: A buried heap of rubbish with bubbles rising out of it and a small flame above.

terms.meaning: A place where mixed rubbish is piled up in the open or buried, with no sorting.
terms.example: A hill of mixed rubbish at the edge of a city is a dump.
terms.art: A tall hill of mixed rubbish at the edge of a city with crows circling above.

terms.meaning: Turning used material into new things.
terms.example: A used plastic bottle can be shredded and spun into thread for a shirt.
terms.art: A plastic bottle becoming flakes, then thread, then a folded shirt in three drawings.

terms.meaning: A person who earns a living by collecting, sorting and selling used material.
terms.example: A waste picker sorts bottles, paper and metal into separate sacks and sells each to a dealer.

terms.meaning: A group that is owned and run by its own members, who share the work and the earnings.

terms.meaning: The solid waste that a body passes out after food. Many families call it potty or latrine waste.

terms.art: A plain side view of a toilet pan with a bucket and a mug beside it.

terms.art: A child resting under a blanket while a parent holds out a glass of salty-sweet water.

terms.art: A wide empty field at dawn with a well downhill and a dotted line of rain running to it.

terms.art: A cutaway drawing of a toilet pan with a pipe leading to two brick-lined pits.

terms.art: A street with a manhole cover and a cutaway showing a pipe below.

items: Name of each player at the top of a column.
A row for each turn. Write 2, 1 or 0 points.

rules: There are 36 cards. Each has an item on the front and the answer on the back. Keep the answer side hidden.
On your turn, take the top card and read the front aloud. Say which bin you would put it in, and where it goes next. Then place the card on that bin and turn it over to read the back.
You score 1 point if your bin matches the back. You score 1 more point if your next stop matches the back in the main idea. You do not need the same words.
A card marked Argue card has two answers that can be defended. Say the bin you would choose and give one reason. You score 2 points for any bin with a reason, and 1 point if you give no reason.
A card that holds something sharp, medical or dirty is harmful waste. Say aloud that only a grown-up touches it in real life.
With 2 to 4 players, take turns round the table until the pile is gone. With 4 players, each takes 9 cards.
The game ends when the pile is empty. The player with the most points wins. If there is a tie, the tied players share the win.
Playing alone, turn all 36 cards yourself and add up your points. The most you can score is 72. Try to beat your own score next time.
If you do not agree with the back of a card, say why. Then ask a grown-up what your own town or building does. Your town's rule may be different.

experiments.title: The dustbin count
experiments.question: What is one day of our family's waste made of, and where does each kind go next?
experiments.predict: Before you open anything, guess. Out of all the waste, how much will be wet, how much dry and how much harmful? Say why you think so.
experiments.fair_test: The family collects one whole day of waste in the same bucket, from waking to bedtime. Every item is counted by the same rule. Anything bigger than a thumb counts as one, and a pile of tiny things such as tea leaves counts as one. One day can be unusual, so if you can, repeat the count on a second ordinary day and compare.

schedule.what: Guess the shares, then start the covered bucket and fill it for one whole day.
Sort the waste into three heaps with gloves, count each heap, find where each kind goes next and compare with your guess.

results_table: My guess (big, medium or small heap)
Weight in grams, if you have a scale
experiments.safety: Wear gloves or use kitchen tongs and shoes. Do the sorting outdoors, on a balcony or on a bathroom floor over newspaper, never in the kitchen. A grown-up alone handles glass, blades, medicines, batteries, nappies, pads and bandages, and the child counts them from the closed bag without touching. Wash hands and forearms with soap for 20 seconds afterwards.

rubber gloves or kitchen tongs
a small bag or carton marked Harmful, kept apart for the grown-up

a kitchen scale (an extra, if you have one)
soap, water and a towel
paper, a pencil and coloured pencils

setup.caption: 4. Count each heap. Draw an arrow from each heap to where it goes next.

flow.do: Give your child three circles of the same size drawn on paper. Ask your child to colour each circle to show how much of the day's waste will be wet, dry and harmful.
flow.say: Think about everything we throw away today. How much do you think will be food and peels, how much paper and plastic, and how much dangerous stuff? Colour in your guess, and tell me why.
flow.kid: Colour in your guess for wet, dry and harmful. Say why you think so.

ask.q: Which kind do you think will be biggest, and why?
good: Wet, because we cook and eat every day and peel things.
Dry, because of packets, bottles and paper.
Any answer with a reason from the family's own day is a good answer.

flow.parent: Do not give the real shares. A wrong guess is the best start. Keep the drawing to compare at the end.

flow.do: Set a bucket with a lid or a plate over it by the kitchen. Tell the whole family that today everything goes into it as usual. Anything sharp, medical or dirty goes into the small marked bag, handled by a grown-up only.
flow.say: From now till bedtime, everything we throw away goes in this bucket. Sharp, medical and nappy waste goes in the small bag, and a grown-up puts it there.
flow.kid: Put your waste in the bucket today. Never put sharp things in it yourself.
flow.parent: In hot weather, cover the bucket and keep it away from the food shelf, because wet waste smells and brings flies within hours. If the family makes very little waste, keep the bucket for a second day. A small heap is a real result.
flow.wait: Leave the bucket covered for one day, from waking to bedtime.

flow.do: The next morning, spread 4 or 5 sheets of newspaper on a balcony, terrace or bathroom floor. Put on gloves, or pick up tongs. Open the marked bag only outdoors and count the items from the closed top without opening the sealed packets.
flow.say: Today we find out the truth about our bin. Gloves on first, and nothing is touched with bare hands.
flow.kid: Put on gloves or pick up tongs. Wait for the grown-up before opening anything.
flow.parent: If anyone has dust allergy or asthma, a cloth mask helps. Do not sort in the kitchen. If the bucket smells strongly, sort quickly and cover it again.

flow.do: Tip the bucket onto the newspaper. Using gloves or tongs, lift each item to one of three plates or sheets: wet, dry and harmful. Items that are stuck together, such as a leaf plate with food on it, go to the kind that most of the item is. Leave glass, blades, medicine and anything wet from the toilet to the grown-up.
flow.say: Pick up one thing at a time. Say what it is, say where it goes, and put it down. If you are not sure, say both bins and why.
flow.kid: Lift one thing at a time with tongs. Say the bin before you put it down.

ask.q: Which item was hardest to place, and why?
good: Items made of two things stuck together, such as a shiny chips packet or a leaf plate with food on it.
Items that were wet and dry at once, such as a curd cup with curd in it.

flow.parent: Mixed items are the real finding. Do not hurry the child to the right answer. Say 'Both are possible. What would each choice cause?' Allow only items you can see clearly. If glass or something sharp comes up, stop and let a grown-up pick it up.

flow.do: Count the items in each heap and write the numbers in the table. If you have a scale, weigh each heap on its plate, then take away the plate's weight. Wrap up the harmful heap again. Compare the heaps by eye: which one is biggest, and by how much?
flow.say: Count each heap by tens, and write the number. Is it what you guessed?
flow.kid: Count the items in each heap. Write each number in the table.
flow.parent: Do not worry if your counts are very different from the national picture of about half wet. Cities and homes are different, and so are the days. For a scale, weigh the paper too and take it away.

check.q: A bucket holds 20 wet items, 12 dry items and 3 harmful items. What share is wet?
check.why: 20 out of 35 items is a little more than half. If you chose the first, you may have compared 20 with 12 and 3 instead of the total of 35.

flow.do: For each heap, find out where it goes next and who meets it there. Ask the family, the person who collects waste, or the housing society. If nobody knows, use the usual route and write that nobody here knew.
flow.say: Where does this heap go when it leaves our door? Who touches it next? Draw a line to each place.
flow.kid: Draw an arrow from each heap to the next place. Draw who is waiting there.

ask.q: Who meets your wet waste next, and who meets your dry waste?
good: Wet: a compost pit, a gas plant, a cow or crow, or a dump. Dry: a waste picker, a dealer and a factory.
If a heap goes to a dump, say that nobody here separates it, and ask why.

flow.parent: The usual routes are these. Wet waste goes to a compost pit or a gas plant, or to a dump. Dry waste goes to a waste picker, a dealer and a factory. Harmful waste goes to a sealed bag and a special collection point. Your own town may send it all to one place. That is also a real finding.

flow.do: Put everything back in the right bins. Wash your hands and forearms with soap for 20 seconds. Then compare the real counts with the guess drawing from the beginning and write three sentences in the record.
flow.say: Was your guess close? What would you change in how our family throws things away tomorrow?
flow.kid: Wash your hands with soap. Write what you thought, what you counted and why.
flow.parent: What the test cannot tell us: one day can be an odd day, such as a festival or a guest. It also does not show what happens once the truck takes the waste away. Ask the child how they would find out.
flow.think: If we change one thing, which heap will shrink?

experiments.title: Water or soap? The turmeric hand test
experiments.question: Does washing hands with plain water get as much off as washing with soap?
experiments.predict: Guess before you wash. Will plain water or soap leave less yellow on your hands, or will they be the same? Say why you think so.
experiments.fair_test: Both palms get the same amount of turmeric and oil. Each hand is washed for the same 20 seconds, with the same amount of water. Only the soap changes. Because one hand may rub harder than the other, the experiment is done twice, with the hands swapped the second time. Each wash is checked by wiping on a clean white tissue.
results_table: Yellow left on the tissue (none, a little, a lot)
Yellow left under the nails or in the lines of the palm (none, a little, a lot)

materials.item: turmeric powder
a few drops of any cooking oil
a bar of soap or liquid handwash
white tissues or white paper napkins
a mug and a bowl of clean water, or a running tap
a phone or clock that shows seconds
a plate of water and a pinch of black pepper (for the extra step)
paper and a pencil

experiments.record: Fill in the table for both tries. Then write what you thought, what you saw, and why you think soap did what it did. Add one sentence about what turmeric cannot tell you about real germs.
experiments.context: In this experiment you use turmeric in place of germs and wash one hand with plain water and the other with soap. You compare what is left, and you find out why soap does a job that water alone cannot.

setup.art: A child's two palms held up with a spot of yellow turmeric and oil on each one, beside a small bowl of turmeric.
setup.caption: 1. Rub the same amount of turmeric and oil on both palms.
