setup.art: A child washing one hand under a mug of water and the other hand with soap, with a clock showing 20 seconds.
setup.caption: 2. Wash one hand with water only and the other with soap, each for 20 seconds.

setup.art: Two white tissues side by side, one with a faint yellow smudge and one with a strong yellow smudge, and a child pointing at them.
setup.caption: 3. Wipe each hand on its own white tissue and compare the yellow.

flow.do: Put out a pinch of turmeric, a few drops of oil, soap, tissues, water and a clock. Wear old clothes, because turmeric stains. Keep turmeric away from eyes.
flow.say: Today the turmeric is pretending to be germs. Our job is to find which way of washing takes the most away.
flow.kid: Put on old clothes. Lay everything out on the table.
flow.parent: If you have no turmeric, use a drop of washable poster paint instead. Do the test over a sink or a bowl so that spills are easy to clean.

flow.do: Mix a pinch of turmeric (about a quarter of a teaspoon) with 3 or 4 drops of oil to make a paste. Rub half on each palm, spreading it into the lines of the hand and a little under the nails.
flow.say: Rub the yellow paste on both hands. It is the same on each hand.
flow.kid: Rub the same yellow paste on both palms.

ask.q: Which will take off more yellow, plain water or soap? Why?
good: Soap, because it grips the oil and lifts it away.
Plain water, because water washes things off. Both are fair guesses. We will test them.

flow.parent: Do not say which is right. Ask for a guess and a reason, and write them down.

flow.do: Wash the left hand with plain water only for 20 seconds, rubbing like normal. Wash the right hand with soap for 20 seconds, rubbing like normal, then rinse it with the same amount of water. Wipe each hand on its own white tissue and mark the tissues Water and Soap.
flow.say: Rub for 20 seconds on each hand. Count slowly. Then wipe each hand on its own tissue.
flow.kid: Wash one hand with water and one with soap. Count to 20. Wipe each hand on a tissue.
flow.parent: A 20-second wash is about the time it takes to sing a short song twice. Use a timer so that both times match.

flow.do: Look at the two tissues and at both hands, especially the nails and the lines of the palms. Write the results in the table. Then repeat with the hands swapped: soap on the left hand and water on the right.
flow.say: Which tissue is more yellow? Which hand still has yellow in the lines? Now swap hands and do it again, so that it is a fair test.
flow.kid: Look at the tissues. Which one is more yellow? Swap hands and try again.
flow.parent: Normally the soap tissue is clearly cleaner. If both tissues look the same, make the paste thicker with a little more oil. Turmeric on a dry hand simply falls off.

check.q: Why do we swap hands in the second try?
options: One hand might rub harder than the other.
Soap works only on the left hand.
check.why: One hand may be stronger or rub harder. Swapping hands tests the washing and not the hand. If you chose the second option, remember that a second try checks a result, it does not mean the first was wrong.

flow.do: Extra step. Sprinkle black pepper on a plate of water so that the pepper floats. Touch the middle with a clean finger and watch. Then touch the same place with a finger that has a little soap on it.
flow.say: Pepper floats like tiny germs on water. First touch with a dry finger. Now touch with a soapy finger. What happened?
flow.kid: Touch the pepper water with a plain finger. Then touch it with a soapy finger. What do you see?

ask.q: What did the soapy finger do to the pepper?
good: The pepper rushed to the edges of the plate.
The soap changed how the water holds together, and the pepper was pushed away.

flow.parent: A plain finger moves the pepper only a little. The soapy finger sends the pepper skating to the edge. Soap works on the film of the water and on oil. It is why soap lifts germs and oil off skin, while plain water only rinses some of them. The turmeric is not a germ, so this test cannot show how many real germs are left. It shows only that soap helps. Ask the child what else they would test.

flow.do: Wash the hands properly with soap and clean the table. Put the tissues in the dry bin and wash the turmeric from any clothes soon.
flow.say: Now wash with soap, like you would after the toilet, and in the way you would before eating.
flow.kid: Wash your hands with soap for 20 seconds.
flow.parent: Remind the child of the moments when washing counts most: after the toilet, before eating, and after touching waste.

activities.title: Swept clean? Follow the dust
activities.context: This activity follows a heap of swept dust to see what happens when dust is only moved. You compare it with dust that is lifted into a dustpan, and you decide which one made the place cleaner.

materials.item: a broom and a dustpan
a sheet of newspaper
a teaspoon of atta, if your floor is very clean
a hand fan or a folded card
paper and a pencil

schedule.what: Sweep a small patch, push the dust to a doorway, fan it, then lift the same kind of dust into a dustpan and compare.

activities.record: Draw two paths on one sheet. Draw where the pushed dust ended up, and where the dust in the dustpan ended up. Write one sentence saying which made the place cleaner and why.
activities.safety: Sweep near an open door or a window. A child who sneezes with dust wears a cloth over nose and mouth. Wash hands afterwards.

setup.art: A child sweeping a small square of floor with a broom, with two heaps of dust at a doorway.
setup.caption: 1. Sweep one patch of floor into a heap at the doorway.

setup.art: A hand fan blowing a gentle breeze towards a heap of dust, with a few specks drifting back across the floor.
setup.caption: 2. Fan gently, like a breeze, and watch where the dust goes.

setup.art: A dustpan lifting a second heap of dust and tipping it into a bin.
setup.caption: 3. Lift a second heap into the dustpan and tip it into the dry bin.

flow.do: Choose a patch of floor about one metre across near a doorway. Ask your child to sweep it into one heap beside the door. If the floor is spotless, sprinkle a teaspoon of atta first.
flow.say: This heap is the dust from our floor. Where do you think it will go next?
flow.kid: Sweep one patch of floor into a heap by the door.

ask.q: Where will the heap go if nobody picks it up?
good: Out of the door into the street, onto a shoe, into the air, or onto a plate.
Any answer with a reason is good.

flow.parent: Dust is always there, so you will not run out. Open the door or window first so there is a little air moving.

flow.do: Ask your child to fan the heap gently, as if with a breeze or a few footsteps, and watch the dust. Ask what the dust did and where it went.
flow.say: Fan the heap a little. What does the dust do? Could this dust land on someone's food?
flow.kid: Fan the dust gently. Watch where it travels.

ask.q: What happened to the dust when the air moved?
good: It floated up and spread over the floor again.
It moved to a new place. Sweeping it to the door only moved it.

flow.parent: Do not blow hard. The point is that light dust travels with a little wind, with feet and with brooms.

flow.do: Sweep a second heap the same way. This time, lift it into a dustpan and tip it into the dry bin or onto the newspaper. Ask your child to compare the two heaps: which one can still travel?
flow.say: This heap is in the dustpan. Can it travel now? Which heap made the room cleaner, the first or the second?
flow.kid: Lift the second heap into the dustpan. Tip it in the bin.

ask.q: Which heap can still travel, and which cannot?
good: The pushed heap can travel. The dustpan heap is in a bin and goes where the collector takes it.
Clean means a harmful thing is kept from reaching people. Only the second heap did that.

flow.parent: Ask: 'If I swept my dust onto the road, is the road cleaner or dirtier?'

flow.do: Ask your child to draw the two paths. Then ask which neighbour they would rather have: a house that sweeps dust out, or a house that bins it.
flow.say: Draw where each heap ended up. Which neighbour would you rather have?
flow.kid: Draw two paths. Write which way is cleaner.
flow.think: If everyone sweeps their dust to the road, where does it all end up?

activities.title: Ask the person who cleans: three questions and a thank-you
activities.context: This activity is a short, polite talk with a person who cleans your street, building or school. You learn what the work is, what makes it harder, and what small thing the family could do to help.

materials.item: paper and a pencil
a small thank-you card made by the child, or a drawing

schedule.what: Plan three questions, ask them with a grown-up beside you, say thank you, and write down what you learned.

activities.record: Write the three questions and the answers. Add one thing that surprised you and one small thing your family can do tomorrow.

setup.art: A child and a parent at a table writing three questions on a sheet of paper.
setup.caption: 1. Write three questions about the work.

setup.art: A child and a grown-up speaking politely to a woman with a broom outside a gate, with the broom resting on her shoulder.
setup.caption: 2. Ask the three questions at a good moment, with a grown-up beside you.

setup.art: A child handing a hand-drawn thank-you card to a sanitation worker.
setup.caption: 3. Say thank you and give your card.

flow.do: Help your child choose a person to talk to. It could be the person who sweeps your street, the collector who comes for waste, a school cleaner or a building's helper. Write three questions together. A good start: What do you do first each morning? What is the hardest part of the work? What would make it easier for you?
flow.say: We are going to ask a person who cleans for us three questions. We want to understand the work.
flow.kid: Write three questions to ask the person who cleans.
flow.parent: Choose a quiet time, not the busiest part of their work. Ask first whether they have a few minutes. Do not ask about caste, pay or family. If you cannot meet anyone, ask a grown-up who cleans at home, or read the story in this lesson.

flow.do: Go together and ask politely. Let your child ask the questions. Listen to the answers without correcting. If the person prefers not to talk, thank them and leave.
flow.say: Say hello first. Then ask your first question. Listen to the whole answer.
flow.kid: Say hello. Ask your three questions. Listen carefully.

ask.q: What did the worker say is hardest, and what would help?
good: Mixed waste, sharp things in the bag, no gloves, smell, and having no place to rest.
Rinsed, sorted waste would help. Any honest answer from the conversation is good.

flow.parent: Stand beside the child and keep your phone away. Do not take photos of the worker's face unless they say yes.

flow.do: Help your child say thank you for the time and give the card, or simply say thank you. Then write down the answers straight away.
flow.say: Say thank you. Their time is worth a lot.
flow.kid: Say thank you. Give your card.
flow.parent: Thanks said plainly, to the person's face, matters as much as a gift.

flow.do: At home, ask your child to read the answers. Choose one small thing the family can do from tomorrow. It could be rinsing dry waste, wrapping blades or putting waste out on time.
flow.say: Which one thing will we change? Who will remind us?
flow.kid: Choose one thing our family will do from tomorrow.
flow.parent: Choose one thing the family can keep. A small change that lasts is better than a big one that stops.
flow.think: Who cleans for you, and have you ever said thank you?

activities.title: A mug of rain: what does a drain carry?
activities.context: This activity makes a tiny street and a tiny drain on a tray. You pour one mug of water as rain and watch what the water carries to the bowl at the bottom.

materials.item: a steel or plastic tray, or a large plate
3 or 4 books to tilt the tray
a bowl or steel pot
10 small pieces of torn tissue or paper
a spoon of soil
a dozen grains of rice
a mug of clean water
a clear glass or plastic glass

schedule.what: Tilt a tray, place bits at the top, pour a mug of water as rain, and see what lands in the bowl.

activities.record: Draw the tray with an arrow for the water. Colour the things that reached the bowl and leave the others white. Write one sentence about what a real drain would carry to a river.

setup.art: A tray tilted on a pile of books with a bowl at the low end, and scraps of paper, soil and rice at the top.
setup.caption: 1. Tilt the tray. Put the bowl at the low end and the bits at the top.

setup.art: A hand pouring a mug of water slowly over the top of the tray.
setup.caption: 2. Pour the mug of water slowly over the top, like rain.

setup.art: A glass of cloudy water from the bowl held up next to a glass of clear tap water.
setup.caption: 3. Compare the bowl's water with a glass of clean tap water.

flow.do: Work on a table, a balcony floor or a bathroom floor. Tilt the tray on 3 or 4 books so that one end is about 8 centimetres higher. Put the bowl under the low end. Put the paper bits, the soil and the rice in a line near the top.
flow.say: This tray is our street. The bowl is our river. The bits are what people dropped.
flow.kid: Tilt the tray on the books. Put the bits at the top.

ask.q: What do you think the rain will carry to the bowl?
good: Paper and soil, which are light. Rice may stay.
Any guess with a reason about weight or floating is good.

flow.parent: If the tray is flat, add another book. The tilt should be steep enough that water runs down the whole tray in about two seconds.

flow.do: Pour one mug of water slowly over the top, as steadily as you can, so that it runs down in a sheet. Watch which bits travel and which stay.
flow.say: Now it is raining. Pour slowly and watch.
flow.kid: Pour the water slowly over the top. Watch the bits.

ask.q: Which bits reached the bowl, and which stayed?
good: Paper and soil reached the bowl. Rice grains mostly stayed.
Light things float and travel. Heavy things stay unless the water is fast.

flow.parent: Rice grains may move a little if the tilt is steep. That is also a finding. Say that heavier things travel in a stronger flow, such as a monsoon downpour.

flow.do: Hold up the bowl's water beside a glass of clean tap water. Ask your child to look, and to say what the bowl's water holds that the tap water does not.
flow.say: Look at the water in the bowl. Would you drink it? What is in it that was not there before?
flow.kid: Compare the bowl's water with clean water. What is different?

ask.q: What does the water carry that it did not hold before?
good: Soil, paper bits and tiny pieces that make it cloudy.
A real drain also carries oil, soap and germs, which we cannot see here.

flow.parent: Real street water carries far more than this. The drain does not clean the water. It only moves it.

flow.do: Ask your child to colour the picture. Then pour the water down a drain or onto a plant. Put the paper bits and rice in the dry bin or compost.
flow.say: Where did our rain-water go? Where would it go in a real street?
flow.kid: Draw the water's path. Colour the things that travelled.
flow.parent: Put the soil back in a pot or on a plant.
flow.think: If the bowl were a river and the paper were plastic, who would meet it downstream?

activities.title: A ten-minute clean-up of one corner, and a count by kind
activities.context: This activity is a short clean-up of one shared corner with gloves, a bag and a grown-up. You pick up only safe dry litter, count it by kind and read what the labels say. Do this if you have a corner outside, a society lane, a school edge or a park nearby.

materials.item: rubber gloves or garden gloves, 1 pair for each person
kitchen tongs or a litter picker
a strong cloth bag or a bucket for dry waste
a pencil and a sheet of paper for tallying
soap and water to wash afterwards

schedule.what: Choose a corner, draw how it looks, pick up safe dry litter for ten minutes, count it, sort it and wash your hands.

activities.record: Draw the corner before and after. Make a tally by kind: bottle, wrapper, cup, bag, paper and other. Write the three kinds you found most of, and the brand names that came up most often.
activities.safety: A grown-up goes along and chooses the place. Wear gloves and closed shoes. Pick up only dry wrappers, paper, plastic and cans. Never pick up glass, needles, syringes, blades, medicine, nappies, pads, bandages, dead animals, anything wet from a toilet or anything you are unsure of. Show these to the grown-up and leave them. Stay away from roads, water and slopes.

setup.art: A child and a parent in gloves standing at the edge of a lane with litter on one side, looking at a bag and tongs.
setup.caption: 1. Choose one small corner and make a plan with a grown-up.

setup.art: A child in gloves using tongs to lift a bottle into a cloth bag while a parent watches.
setup.caption: 2. Pick up only safe dry litter for ten minutes.

setup.art: A row of litter sorted on newspaper by kind with tally marks beside each kind.
setup.caption: 3. Sort what you picked into kinds and count each kind.

flow.do: Choose a small corner, about the size of a classroom, in a place where you have permission. It could be your lane, the edge of your school, a park or a corridor. Draw how it looks before you start. Show the child the safety rules and the things never to touch.
flow.say: We will pick up a small corner for ten minutes. Gloves on, shoes on, and ask me before you pick up anything you are not sure of.
flow.kid: Draw the corner. Put on gloves. Listen to the rules.
flow.parent: Ask the housing society, school or neighbours first if it is not your own space. If you have no corner nearby, use a school corridor or your building's compound. Check the corner yourself first for glass and sharp things.

flow.do: Set a timer for ten minutes. Ask your child to pick up safe dry litter with tongs or gloves. Hold the bag together. If the child finds glass, a needle, a syringe or anything wet, leave it and tell a grown-up.
flow.say: Use the tongs. Put each thing in the bag. Stop and call me if it is sharp, wet, medical or you are not sure.
flow.kid: Pick up dry litter with tongs. Stop and call a grown-up if it is sharp or wet.
flow.parent: Stay close to the child. Do not take away the child's wish to help, but keep the rules firm. Put sharp or dirty things aside yourself with a stick or a pair of tongs.

flow.do: Tip the bag onto newspaper. Sort by kind into piles, and make a tally of each kind. Read the brand names on the labels and make a tally of the most common ones. Then sort what can be recycled into the dry bin.
flow.say: What did we find the most of? Which names did we see the most? Whose packet is it?
flow.kid: Sort the litter into kinds. Make a tally of each.

ask.q: Which kind did you find the most of, and why do you think so?
good: Wrappers and bottles, because most things come in them and people drop them while eating or walking.
A kind that came from one brand or one shop nearby.

flow.parent: Counting brand names shows which packaging ends up on the ground. It can lead to a letter to the company or the shop.

flow.do: Draw the corner again. Wash hands and forearms with soap for 20 seconds. Ask your child whether the corner will stay clean, and what would help it stay clean.
flow.say: Will this corner stay clean? What would help? A bin? A sign? A neighbour?
flow.kid: Draw the corner after the clean-up. Wash your hands with soap.
flow.parent: Cleaning one corner is useful. Keeping it clean needs a bin, regular collection or neighbours who look after it. The lesson explains why.
flow.think: One person cleaned this corner today. What would it take to keep it clean tomorrow?

activities.title: An old T-shirt becomes a carry bag, with no sewing
activities.context: This activity turns a worn-out cotton T-shirt into a shopping bag using only scissors and knots. It is one way to refuse a thin carry bag and reuse cloth that would have been thrown away.

materials.item: an old cotton T-shirt that will not be worn again
sharp scissors, for the grown-up
a ruler
chalk or a pencil
1 kilogram of rice, dal or books to test the bag

schedule.what: Mark and cut the T-shirt, tie the fringe, and test the bag with a kilogram of rice.

activities.record: Draw your bag. Write how many knots you tied, how much weight it held, and what you would change.
activities.safety: The grown-up does all the cutting with scissors. The child marks, ties and tests.

setup.art: A T-shirt laid flat with chalk lines marking the neck curve, the sleeves and a row of strips along the bottom.
setup.caption: 1. Mark the neck, the sleeves and the bottom strips with chalk.

setup.art: A pair of hands tying two strips from the front and back of a T-shirt in a double knot.
setup.caption: 2. Tie each front strip to the back strip with a double knot.

setup.art: A finished T-shirt bag filled with vegetables and held by its shoulder straps.
setup.caption: 3. Turn the T-shirt over and test with a kilogram of rice.

flow.do: Lay the T-shirt flat. Use chalk to draw a wide curve across each side of the neck so that it becomes a scoop. Mark a line across the bottom, 8 centimetres from the hem, and strips 2 centimetres wide along it from side to side.
flow.say: This T-shirt is going to be a bag. We mark where the grown-up will cut.
flow.kid: Lay the T-shirt flat. Draw the lines with chalk.
flow.parent: Any cotton T-shirt works. Knit cloth does not fray, so no hem is needed.

flow.do: A grown-up cuts off the sleeves along the seams and along the neck curve. Then the grown-up cuts the bottom strips, through both layers, up to the 8 centimetre line.
flow.say: The grown-up cuts. You hold the cloth flat.
flow.kid: Hold the shirt flat while the grown-up cuts.
flow.parent: Cut through both layers at once so that front and back strips match. Cut the strips up to, and not past, the line.

flow.do: Tie each front strip to the strip behind it in a double knot, working from one side to the other. Pull each knot tight. At the end, check that no gap is left between any two knots, by pulling the bottom of the bag a little wide.
flow.say: Tie a front strip to the one behind it. Tie it twice. Pull it tight. Go along the whole bottom.
flow.kid: Tie each pair of strips twice. Pull tight. Go from side to side.

ask.q: Why do we tie each pair twice?
good: One knot can slip under weight. A double knot holds.
Any answer about a knot coming loose is a good answer.

flow.parent: Check for gaps. A gap smaller than a rice grain holds, but bigger gaps spill lentils.

flow.do: Turn the T-shirt inside out so the knots are inside, and test the bag with a kilogram of rice, dal or books. Lift it by the straps.
flow.say: Put in the rice. Lift the bag. Does it hold?
flow.kid: Fill the bag with rice. Lift it. Does it hold?
flow.parent: If the bag leaks, tie another knot over the gap. A small gap is easy to mend.

check.q: The bag leaks rice at the corners. What is the best fix?
options: Tie each corner strip a second time.
check.why: Leaks come from gaps between knots. Tying a second knot at the corners closes the gap. Using less rice would only hide the gap.

flow.do: Ask your child to hang the bag by the door, and to say how many thin carry bags it can replace in a year.
flow.say: Where will we keep it so that it goes with us every time?
flow.kid: Hang the bag by the door.
flow.think: A cloth bag only helps if it goes to the market every time. What would make you remember?

projects.title: Two peels, two futures: a jar with air and a jar without
projects.context: In this project you put the same peels in two jars, one with air and soil and one packed under water. For three weeks you look, smell from a distance and measure, to see what living beings do to a peel in each place.

materials.item: 2 clear plastic jars or containers with wide mouths, about 500 millilitres each
12 small pieces of vegetable or fruit peel, each about the size of a thumb (banana, potato, carrot, cucumber or apple)
2 handfuls of garden or pot soil
a handful of torn dry paper or dry leaves
a piece of old cloth and a rubber band
a marker and masking tape for labels
a ruler
rubber gloves, a notebook and a pencil

schedule.what: Set up jar A with soil, peels and dry paper under a cloth, and jar B with the same peels pressed under water.
Look at both jars from the outside. Write the changes.
Look at both jars, waft the smell gently, and write what you notice.
Look, smell and measure the largest piece in each jar.
Compare the jars, then empty them safely and wash your hands.

projects.record: Keep a table with the day, what each jar looks like, how it smells and the length of the biggest peel in centimetres. Draw each jar on days 1, 7 and 21. Then write three sentences: what I thought, what I saw and why.
projects.safety: Do not close either lid tightly, because gas can build up. Do not put your nose close to the jars. Wave the smell towards you with your hand. If you see black or green mould, do not open the jar. Ask a grown-up to empty it outdoors. Wear gloves to empty the jars and wash hands with soap afterwards.

setup.art: Two clear jars on a shelf labelled A and B, with soil, peels and dry paper in jar A and peels under water in jar B.
setup.caption: 1. Fill jar A with soil, peels and dry paper. Fill jar B with the same peels and water.

setup.art: Jar A covered with a cloth and a rubber band, and jar B with a loose lid sitting on top.
setup.caption: 2. Cover A with cloth so air gets in. Rest a lid loosely on B.

setup.art: Two jars on a notebook page with a drawing of each and a ruler beside the peel.
setup.caption: 3. Draw and measure the jars on days 1, 3, 7, 14 and 21.

setup.art: Two jars after three weeks, one with dark crumbly soil and small peels and one with cloudy water and floating peels.
setup.caption: 4. Day 21: compare the jars and empty them.

flow.do: Label two jars A and B. Cut 12 pieces of peel into thumb-sized pieces and put 6 in each jar. For jar A, put in a layer of soil, then 6 peels, then a handful of torn dry paper. Sprinkle a little water so that the jar is damp but not wet. Cover with cloth and a rubber band. For jar B, press the other 6 peels to the bottom and fill the jar with water to the top. Rest the lid loosely on top. Put both jars together on a shelf out of the sun.
flow.say: These two jars hold the same peels. One has air and soil. One has no air. What do you think will happen to each peel?
flow.kid: Put the same peels in both jars. Add soil and paper to A. Add water to B.

ask.q: What do you think will happen in jar A and jar B, and why?
good: In A, the peels will shrink, go dark and turn to soil, because tiny living beings eat them with air.
In B, the water will smell and look cloudy, because different bacteria work without air.

flow.parent: Use a warm shelf, about 25 to 35 degrees. In cold weather, things go slower, and it may take 10 extra days. Keep both jars in the same place so the test is fair.

flow.do: Look at both jars from the outside. Draw them and write what you see. Do not open them.
flow.say: Look closely. What has changed in A? What has changed in B? How is the water?
flow.kid: Look at both jars. Draw what you see. Do not open them.
flow.parent: By day 3, jar B often has small bubbles, cloudy water and some froth. Jar A may have some white threads. Both are normal.
flow.wait: Leave the jars for two days.

flow.do: Look and measure again. Wave the smell towards you with a hand from about an arm's length from each jar. Write one word for each smell, such as earthy, sour, sweet or none. Measure the largest peel in jar A without opening, through the plastic.
flow.say: Smell it from far away, with your hand like a fan. Which smells like soil? Which smells sour?
flow.kid: Wave the smell towards you. Choose one word for each smell.
flow.parent: A white fuzz on the peels in A is fungus, a normal part of rotting. Black or green mould in large patches means the damp is too high. Ask a grown-up to empty it.
flow.wait: Leave the jars for another week.

flow.do: Look, smell and measure the largest piece in each jar. Write what is different from day 7.
flow.say: What is smaller? What changed colour? Which jar smells stronger, and why do you think so?
flow.kid: Look, smell and measure. Write what changed.

ask.q: Which jar smells stronger now, and why?
good: Jar B smells stronger, sour or like rotten eggs, because bacteria that live without air make smelly gases.
Jar A smells more like soil, because bacteria with air make little smell.

flow.wait: Leave the jars for one more week.

flow.do: With gloves on, empty jar A onto soil in a pot or the wet waste bin. A grown-up pours jar B into a toilet or onto soil far from the house, and puts the peels in the wet bin. Wash the jars. Compare the two drawings and write three sentences.
flow.say: Now compare jar A and jar B. Which one turned into soil? Which one was a smelly mess? What is the difference?
flow.kid: Wash your hands with soap. Write three sentences about what you found.

ask.q: What do jars A and B tell you about a dump with no air?
good: In a dump with no air, wet waste rots in a smelly way and gives off methane, as in jar B.
A heap with air becomes soil, as in jar A.

flow.parent: What the test cannot tell us: a jar is not a real dump or a real compost heap. Real heaps are hotter, bigger and have worms. Ask the child how they would change the test to be closer to the real thing.

projects.title: A week of less: refuse and reuse
projects.context: In this project the family counts the wrappers, bottles and thin bags it throws away on one ordinary day. Then you try three ways of making less waste for four days, and count again to see what changed.

materials.item: a sheet of paper stuck near the dustbin, and a pencil on a string
a cloth bag, a steel bottle or a steel tiffin from home
ruled paper for a table
coloured pencils for the graph

schedule.what: Make a tally sheet and count every wrapper, bottle, thin bag and cup thrown away in the day.
Choose three ways to make less waste.
Try your three ways. Mark each time you manage it.
Try your three ways. Mark each time you manage it.
Try your three ways. Mark each time you manage it.
Try your three ways. Mark each time you manage it.
Count again for one day, draw both counts as bars and talk about what was hard.

projects.record: Keep a table with the day, the number of single-use things thrown away and the ways you tried. Draw two bars, one for day 1 and one for day 7. Write what got easier, what stayed hard and who could change that.

setup.art: A tally sheet taped beside a dustbin with a pencil hanging from a string and some tally marks.
setup.caption: 1. Tape a tally sheet beside the bin. Make a mark for each wrapper, bottle, cup or thin bag.

setup.art: A cloth bag, a steel bottle and a tiffin lined up beside a door on a hook.
setup.caption: 2. Choose three ways of making less waste, and put what you need by the door.

setup.art: Two bars of different heights drawn on a graph, one for day 1 and one for day 7, with a child pointing at them.
setup.caption: 3. Day 7: count again and draw the two bars.

flow.do: Tape a sheet of paper beside the dustbin. Explain that everyone makes a mark each time they throw away a wrapper, a bottle, a cup, a thin bag or a plastic spoon. Choose an ordinary day. Do not touch the waste to count. Count at the moment of throwing.
flow.say: Today we will count every wrapper, bottle and thin bag that we throw away. We just count. We do not change anything yet.
flow.kid: Make a mark on the sheet each time you throw away a wrapper or a bottle.
flow.parent: Pick an ordinary day. A birthday or festival would make an unusual count. If the family forgets some marks, say so on the sheet. A rough count is fine.

flow.do: Show your child these ways. Carry a steel bottle. Say no to a straw or spoon. Carry a cloth bag to the shop. Use a steel tiffin. Use a plate and not a disposable one. Mend something. Ask your child to choose three.
flow.say: Which three can we really do? Not the ones that sound good, but the ones we will do.
flow.kid: Choose three ways to make less waste. Say why you chose them.

ask.q: Which three ways will you choose, and why?
good: Ones that fit the family's day, such as a bottle, a bag by the door and no straw.
A reason about what the family really does each day.

flow.parent: Pick things the whole family can do. Put the bag and the bottle by the door tonight, because remembering is the hardest part.

flow.do: For four days, try the three ways. Each evening, make a tick for each way you managed. Write down one thing that was hard, such as the shopkeeper giving a bag before you could say no.
flow.say: Did you manage all three today? What stopped you?
flow.kid: Try your three ways each day. Tick the ones you did.

ask.q: What made it hard to say no or to remember?
good: The shop gave a bag first, or the bottle was left at home.
A reason that shows the system around the family, such as a shop that wraps everything.

flow.parent: Do not blame the child. A shop that gives a bag automatically is part of the system. Ask the child what the shop could do instead.

flow.do: On day 7, tally again for one ordinary day. Then draw the two bars on one graph and talk about what changed.
flow.say: Is the bar shorter? By how much? What was easier than you thought? What stayed hard?
flow.kid: Count again today. Draw two bars. Write what changed.
flow.think: What would make the next week's bar even shorter, and who would need to help?

check.q: Day 1 had 24 marks and day 7 had 18. What is the change?
check.why: 24 − 18 = 6 fewer. 6 out of 24 is one quarter. If you chose 24 fewer, you took the whole first count away and forgot the new count.

challenges.title: A sorting corner for a small kitchen: ten seconds, no smell
challenges.context: This is an engineering problem. A family says that sorting waste is a good idea but takes too long and smells. You design a sorting corner for a small kitchen that makes sorting quick, clean and easy for every member of the family.
challenges.problem: Design a corner of a small kitchen. A person must be able to sort one item into wet, dry or harmful waste in less than ten seconds, with no smell and no spill. There is more than one good answer.
constraints: The whole corner must fit in a floor space of 40 centimetres by 40 centimetres.
Use things you can find at home. Do not buy anything new.
The wet waste must be covered, and the harmful waste must be out of a small child's reach.
A child who cannot read must still be able to use it.
Test it with 10 items from the Three Bins cards, or 10 clean real items such as a rinsed cup.
materials: three buckets, boxes or baskets, one with a lid
old newspaper, a cloth bag and a plate to cover a bucket
coloured paper, marker pens and tape

setup.art: A small kitchen floor with a square marked in tape, 40 centimetres on each side.
setup.caption: 1. Mark a 40 by 40 centimetre square in a corner with tape.

setup.art: Three containers inside the square, one with a lid, with drawings stuck to them.
setup.caption: 2. Place three containers and label each with a colour and a drawing.

setup.art: A child with a timer dropping an item into a bin while a parent holds a stopwatch.
setup.caption: 3. Time how long it takes to sort 10 items.

flow.do: Read the problem together. Walk around your kitchen and find a place where waste is thrown now. Draw how it works today. Ask the family which part is hard: the time, the smell, the spills or the thinking.
flow.say: What makes sorting slow or smelly in our kitchen today? Which part would you fix first?
flow.kid: Draw how our kitchen handles waste today. Mark the hardest part.

ask.q: Which part of sorting is the hardest in your kitchen?
good: Smell and flies, no place for the third bin, or not knowing which bin.
Any honest answer from the family is good.

flow.parent: Ask all the family members, including those who do the sorting. The person who empties the bin will know what the problem is.

flow.do: Build the corner using what you have. Mark the square, place the three containers, add labels with a colour and a drawing, and cover the wet one. Make the harmful container a small box with a lid, kept up high or behind a door.
flow.say: Where will each bin go? How will you tell them apart without reading?
flow.kid: Build your corner. Label each bin with a colour and a drawing.
flow.parent: Put a layer of dry paper at the bottom of the wet bin to soak up water. Rinse dry items first and leave them in a rack to dry. Everything must be at a height the child can reach, apart from the harmful box.

flow.do: Test the corner with 10 items. Time how long it takes to sort each one. Count how many went to the right bin and how many dropped or spilled. Write the numbers.
flow.say: Ready, steady, sort! How long did each one take? Where did you slow down?
flow.kid: Sort 10 items. Time each one. Count the mistakes.

ask.q: Where did the corner slow you down or go wrong?
good: The bins were too close, the labels were hard to see, or a lid was hard to lift.
Any honest problem found by the test is a good finding.

flow.do: Change one thing and test it again. Write what you changed and whether the time fell. Compare with other designs, if more than one family has tried.
flow.say: What will you change? Will it be faster now?
flow.kid: Change one thing. Test it again. Did it help?
flow.think: Which part of sorting did your design make easier, and which part still depends on people?

general: Three buckets or baskets in a row, with a colour on each. Use green, blue and red or black, and put a lid on the wet one.
A layer of dry paper at the bottom of the wet bin to soak up water and cut the smell.
A drying rack by the sink for rinsed curd cups and milk packets, so they go into the dry bin dry.
creative: A picture for each bin, drawn by the child, so that anyone who cannot read can use it.
A fourth box marked Reuse, for jars, cartons and cloth that someone in the family or a neighbour can use again.
A small steel bin with a pedal made from a chappal and a string. A hand with food on it never has to touch the lid.
A hook on the back of the door with a cloth bag for dry waste, so no floor space is needed.
challenges.your_turn: Design and build your own sorting corner, and test it in front of the family. What did you change that made it quicker? What does your design still ask people to remember?

challenges.title: Catch the wrapper, let the water pass: a trap for a street drain
challenges.context: This is an engineering problem. A street drain has to let rain pass and stop wrappers from reaching the river. You use the tilted tray from the drain activity as a tiny street and design a trap for the bottom of it.
challenges.problem: Make a trap that stops at least 8 out of 10 pieces of paper from reaching the bowl. It must still let a whole mug of water through in under 20 seconds. There is more than one good answer.
constraints: Use only things from home. Nothing sharp is used by the child.
A grown-up does all the cutting.
The trap must not stop water for more than 20 seconds.
Test each design three times with the same amount of paper and water, because one try can be a fluke.
Write down how many bits were caught each time.
materials: a tray or large plate tilted on 3 or 4 books, and a bowl at the low end
10 small pieces of torn paper for each test
a tea strainer, a kitchen sieve, an old cotton cloth, or a stiff paper plate with slits cut by a grown-up
a mug of water for each test

setup.art: A tilted tray with a bowl at the end and 10 pieces of paper scattered on the tray.
setup.caption: 1. Set up the tilted tray with the bowl and 10 bits of paper.

setup.art: A tea strainer standing across the end of the tray over the bowl.
setup.caption: 2. Put your trap across the low end of the tray.

setup.art: A mug of water pouring across the tray while a child watches the trap and a parent holds a timer.
setup.caption: 3. Pour a mug of water and time how long it takes to pass.

flow.do: First, test with no trap. Pour a mug of water over the tray with 10 pieces of paper. Count how many paper pieces reach the bowl. Write the numbers.
flow.say: This is the street with no trap. How many wrappers reach the river?
flow.kid: Pour the water. Count the bits in the bowl.

ask.q: How many bits reached the bowl with no trap?
good: Most of them, if the paper was light and the water ran fast.
Any count the child really made is correct.

flow.parent: This is your baseline. It shows how a drain with no grill acts.

flow.do: Choose one trap from the materials, build it across the end of the tray, and test it three times. Each time, count the bits that reached the bowl and time the water.
flow.say: Which trap will you try first? Will the water still go through?
flow.kid: Build a trap. Test it three times. Write the numbers.
flow.parent: A grown-up cuts slits in the paper plate or cup if used. Use the same amount of paper and water each time, and tip the bits out of the bowl between tests.

flow.do: Look at the results. Did your trap stop the bits and let the water pass? Did it clog? Change one thing and test again.
flow.say: Did the bits pile up and stop the water? What would a real drain need to stay clear?
flow.kid: Look at your numbers. Change one thing. Test again.

ask.q: What happened to the trap when the bits piled up?
good: The water slowed or stopped, because the trap clogged.
A real trap needs a person to empty it often.

flow.do: Talk about who would empty a real trap, and when. Ask your child to draw the person.
flow.say: Who will empty the trap every day? What would they need to do the work safely?
flow.kid: Draw the person who empties the trap. Write what they need.
flow.parent: This links to the sanitation workers in the lesson. A machine can help, but only a person can empty it.
flow.think: A trap in a real drain must be cleaned every day. Who does that, and are they paid, safe and thanked?

general: A fine mesh across the end of the tray, such as a tea strainer or a piece of cotton net. The water passes and the paper is caught.
A sieve held at a slope, so that the paper slides to one side instead of piling up.
A second, coarser trap in front of the fine one, so that the big things are caught first.
creative: A tilted bar that nudges the paper to one side, where it falls into a small tray while the water goes on. This works like a self-cleaning grill.
A piece of old dupatta cloth hung over the bowl like a net, which catches the bits and can be washed and used again.
A bin right at the start of the tray, so that the paper is caught before it joins the water at all. This asks whether the trap is needed if nobody drops the wrapper.
challenges.your_turn: Design and test your own trap. What did it catch, and what did it let through? Who in a real city would need to clean it?

challenges.title: A hand-wash station that uses one mug of water and no tap
challenges.context: This is an engineering problem. Many homes, schools and fields have no tap near the toilet. You design a hand-wash station that uses little water and does not need a dirty hand to touch a tap.
challenges.problem: Make a hand-wash station that gives enough water to wash both hands for 20 seconds with soap. It must use less than one mug of water, about 250 millilitres. It must work without touching a tap with a dirty hand. There is more than one good answer.
constraints: Use things from home. A grown-up makes any small holes.
It must hold the soap within reach.
It must be used with one hand or a foot, so that nobody touches the dirty part.
Test with water only, and measure how much water is used in 20 seconds.
Wash the station and the hands with soap afterwards.
materials: a plastic bottle of 1 or 2 litres with a cap, or a plastic jug
a nail or a clean sewing needle and a bit of rope, for the grown-up
a bowl or bucket to catch the water
a soap bar and a piece of string, or a handwash bottle
a measuring cup or a mug marked in millilitres

setup.art: A plastic bottle hanging on a string beside a bucket with a soap bar tied nearby.
setup.caption: 1. Hang a bottle with small holes near a bowl, with the soap tied close.

setup.art: A child tipping the bottle with a foot pedal made from a string and a stick, while water drips out in a thin stream.
setup.caption: 2. Tip the bottle with a string or a foot, so the water pours out.

setup.art: A bowl of used water with a measuring mug beside it showing how much was used.
setup.caption: 3. Measure how much water you used in 20 seconds.

flow.do: Look at the problem and plan. Fill a mug with water and wash your hands in the usual way, and measure how much water you use. Write it down.
flow.say: How much water do we use to wash our hands now? Do we touch the tap with dirty hands?
flow.kid: Wash your hands as usual. Measure the water you used.

ask.q: How much water did a usual wash use?
good: More than one mug if the tap ran the whole time.
Any measured number is good.

flow.parent: Many families find a running tap uses a litre or more. A bucket and mug can use much less.

flow.do: A grown-up makes two or three small holes in the cap of the bottle with a nail or a clean needle. Fill the bottle with water and tip it to see how it pours. Tie a string so that a foot or an elbow can tip it. Tie the soap near the station.
flow.say: The grown-up makes the holes. You tie the string and the soap.
flow.kid: Tie the string and the soap. Wait for the grown-up to make the holes.
flow.parent: A thick needle pushed through the cap makes a small hole. Too many holes make the water run out too fast.

flow.do: Test the station. Wash both hands with soap for 20 seconds. Measure the water used. Check whether each hand needed to touch the bottle.
flow.say: Time it, wash with soap, and rinse. How much water did you use? Did you touch the dirty part?
flow.kid: Wash with your station. Measure the water used.

ask.q: Did your station use less than one mug?
good: Yes, if the holes were small and the bottle was tipped only when needed.
No, if the water ran all the time. The fix is smaller holes or a stop with a finger.

flow.do: Change one thing and test again. Then wash the bottle and your hands with soap.
flow.say: What will you change to use even less water? Why?
flow.kid: Change one thing. Test again. Write how much water you used.
flow.think: Who in a school, a village or a train station would most need a station like yours?

general: A bottle with a few tiny holes in the cap, hung upside down, with a string to tip it. The water falls in a thin stream.
A bucket with a small tap, placed higher than the bowl, and soap on a string.
A mug dipped into a bucket and poured over the hands with the other hand while the first hand holds soap.
creative: A tippy tap that is tilted by a foot pedal made of a stick and a string. No hand touches anything but the soap.
A hanging coconut shell or steel pot with a tiny hole. It drips for as long as you need and stops when you tilt it back.
A bottle with a sprinkle cap and a clip that holds it open, which waters the plants with the used soap water afterwards.
challenges.your_turn: Design and make your own station. How much water did your hand wash use? What would you change if forty children had to use it every morning?

quiz.p: A lane is swept and neat, but an open drain runs beside its hand pump. Is it clean?
opts: No, because germs can reach the water
Yes, because it looks neat
Yes, because the pump still works
quiz.why: Clean means harmful things are kept away from mouths, water and food. A neat lane can still let germs from the drain reach the pump. If you chose yes, you judged by looks and not by where things can travel.

quiz.p: Which place is cleanest in the scientific sense?
opts: A shiny plate wiped with a dirty cloth
A swept house with dust tipped outside
A muddy garden with a covered compost pit
quiz.why: A plate wiped with a dirty cloth gets germs and not fewer, and dust tipped outside has only moved. A covered pit keeps harmful things away from people even though the garden is muddy.

quiz.p: Leftover sambar is tipped onto a pile of newspapers. What is the main problem?
opts: The paper becomes too heavy to lift
Two useful things become one that nobody can use
The sambar will never rot
quiz.why: Soaked paper cannot go to a paper mill, and food full of ink cannot go to compost. If you chose the weight, you saw a small problem and missed that both heaps are spoilt.

quiz.p: Which of these belongs in the harmful bin?
opts: A used bandage
A banana peel
A rinsed milk packet
A cotton rag
quiz.why: A bandage can carry germs and can hurt the person who sorts it, so it is wrapped and kept apart. A peel is wet waste, a clean packet is dry waste, and a rag is dry waste.

quiz.p: Why must a curd cup be rinsed before it goes into dry waste?
opts: Curd melts the plastic
A rinsed cup weighs less to carry
Curd left in it spoils the whole sack
quiz.why: Food left in one cup soaks the paper and plastic around it so a buyer will not take the sack. If you chose melting, remember that curd does not harm plastic, it only makes the sack dirty.

quiz.p: A peel is buried deep in a dump with no air. What do its bacteria give off?
opts: Methane, a gas that burns and traps heat
Compost and warmth, as in a pot
Nothing, because the peel stays whole
quiz.why: Without air, different bacteria take over and make methane. If you chose compost, you described the same peel with air. If you chose nothing, remember that a buried peel still rots.

quiz.p: A compost heap smells bad and rots very slowly. What is the most likely cause?
opts: Too much sunlight
Too little air reaches it
Too many dry leaves
quiz.why: A bad smell means that bacteria without air have taken over. Stirring the heap or adding dry leaves lets air in. Adding more leaves is part of the fix, and not the cause.

quiz.p: Many cholera cases cluster round one water pump. What does that suggest?
opts: Bad smells in the air cause cholera
Cholera germs live only in pumps
Something in the pump's water spreads the illness
quiz.why: A cluster around one source points to the water. Smells were once blamed, because dirty lanes smelled and had illness, but the smell was not the cause.

quiz.p: Which step blocks germs on fingers from reaching a meal?
opts: Washing hands with soap before eating
Spraying scent in the toilet
Closing the window
quiz.why: Germs travel on fingers, and soap lifts them off. Scent hides a smell and does nothing to germs. A closed window does not stop fingers.

quiz.p: Why can spit on a floor harm people who never met the person who spat?
opts: It dries and floats off as steam
Its germs get on shoes, hands and into the air
It makes the floor slippery
quiz.why: Spit can carry germs from the chest and mouth, and shoes, hands and drops spread them. A slippery floor is a different problem. If you chose steam, remember that germs do not vanish when spit dries.

quiz.p: A village has built a toilet for every home. Does that prove nobody goes in the open?
opts: Yes, toilets are always used
Yes, if the toilets are new
Only if the toilets are painted
No, you must also count who uses them
quiz.why: A toilet that is built but not used still leaves the open field. Researchers visited villages to see what people really do, and found that some toilets were not used.

quiz.p: Two surveys of the same villages give different numbers. What is the best first step?
opts: Ask what each survey counted and how
Believe the bigger number
Throw both surveys away
quiz.why: Different counts can both be true. One may count toilets built and the other people using them. Throwing both away loses what each one tells us.

quiz.p: If a town's scavenging birds disappear, what is most likely to happen to dead animals?
opts: They turn into compost at once
Nothing changes at all
They rot longer, and dogs gather to feed
quiz.why: Scavengers remove dead animals fast. Without them, the bodies lie longer, and dogs and flies gather. If you chose nothing, you may have forgotten that scavengers are part of the cleaning.

quiz.p: A sorter is cut by glass hidden in a bag of mixed waste. What would have prevented it?
opts: A heavier bag
Wrapping the glass and marking the bag
Throwing the bag out at night
quiz.why: The sorter cannot see the glass in a mixed bag. Wrapping and marking it tells the next person what is inside. Weight and timing do not make a bag safer.

quiz.p: Which small action cuts the most waste over a whole year?
opts: Putting each thin bag in the blue bin
Using each thin bag twice
Asking the shop for two thin bags
Carrying your own bag and refusing the thin bag
quiz.why: Refusing a thing means that nobody has to collect, sort or bury it. Recycling and reusing a bag twice still use up the bag.

quiz.p: A beach clean-up removed tonnes of waste, but plastic kept arriving. What does this show?
opts: Clean-ups help, and the sources must change too
Clean-ups are pointless
The beach was never really cleaned
quiz.why: The people who clean up do real good, and new plastic arrives while drains and factories keep sending it. Both small actions and bigger changes are needed.

worksheets.title: Sorting, germs and clean (core)
worksheets.context: This sheet checks that you can tell clean from tidy, sort waste, follow a peel and a germ, and choose small actions.

items.p: A place that looks neat is always clean.
items.why: False. A neat lane can have an open drain beside the hand pump. Clean means harmful things cannot reach mouths, water and food.

items.p: Sort each item into the right bin.
items.a: as given
items.why: Food and flowers rot, so they are wet. Cardboard and glass can be recycled, so they are dry. Blades and medicine can hurt people or poison soil, so they are kept apart.

items.p: Why is a banana peel in the dry bin a problem?
opts: It wets and spoils the paper and plastic
It makes the bin too heavy
It turns the plastic yellow
items.why: A wet peel soaks paper, and dirty plastic is hard to sell. If you chose heavy, think about what the buyer sees: a sack that cannot be used.

items.p: India's rules ask every home to keep ____ kinds of waste apart.
items.why: Wet, dry and harmful. Each is handled in a different way.

items.p: Match each helper or thing to what it does for a compost heap.
pairs: a gas that burns and traps heat
items.a: as given
items.why: Compost is made by living beings eating peels with air. Methane is what you get instead when there is no air.

items.p: Put these in order, first to last: what happens to a peel in a compost pot.
a: A chopped peel is put in a pot with dry leaves
Bacteria and fungi start to eat the peel
items.why: The peel is food first, then the eaters arrive, they make warmth as they work, and what is left is compost.

items.p: Cholera spreads because of bad smells.
items.why: False. People once blamed smells because dirty lanes both smelled and had illness. John Snow showed that the cause was in the water, carried from human waste.

items.p: Draw how germs get from a field to a child's mouth. Mark three places to block them.
items.a: A field, then arrows along two or more paths. For example flies to food, rain to a well to a glass, or feet and fingers to a mouth. Blocks are marked with a toilet, a covered plate, safe water or soap.
items.why: There are several paths and each can be blocked. A toilet stops the first step, covering food stops flies, and soap stops fingers.

items.p: A fly lands on an open heap and then on food. What stops this?
opts: Covering food and keeping heaps closed
Washing the floor
Opening a window
items.why: The germs ride on the fly's legs from the heap to the food. Covering food blocks that path. A clean floor or an open window does not.

items.p: Why does a twin-pit toilet have two pits and not one?
items.a: While one pit fills and is used, the other rests for a year or two. In the resting pit, bacteria turn the waste into safe, dry manure. Then the pipe is turned back.
items.why: A strong answer says that one pit is used while the other rests, and that resting is what makes the waste safe.

items.p: A programme that builds toilets has also made sure that people use them.
items.why: False. A toilet can be built and still not used. That is why researchers count who uses toilets, as well as how many were built.

items.p: A family of four makes about 2 kilograms of waste a day. About how many kilograms in 30 days?
items.why: 2 kilograms × 30 days = 60 kilograms.

items.p: Name two living beings who are not humans and who help clear waste. Say what each one does.
items.a: Examples: bacteria and fungi rot peels into compost, vultures clear dead animals, crows pick up scraps, ants carry away crumbs, dung beetles bury dung.
items.why: Many beings do the cleaning. Their work is also part of keeping places clean.

items.p: A rinsed, sorted bag takes five minutes more each day. Two views on who should do that work.

views.says: I pay a collection fee. The truck mixes everything anyway, so my sorting is wasted.

views.who: A waste pickers' cooperative (an imagined view)
views.says: The mixing in the truck is what spoils it. A sorted bag keeps our hands safe and our material saleable.

items.ask: What would make the resident's sorting worth it?
items.a: Answers vary. A strong answer says that sorting only helps if the truck keeps the bags apart. So the resident and the city both have a part.
items.why: Both views are right in part. The resident is right that mixing in the truck cancels the sorting. The cooperative is right that sorting at home is what makes recycling possible.

items.p: Which small action keeps the most waste from ever being made?
opts: Refusing a thing you do not need
Recycling it after one use
Burning it in the street
items.why: If you refuse a thing, it never has to be made, carried, sorted or buried. Recycling needs energy and work. Burning plastic makes harmful smoke.

items.p: Draw one corner of your street. Mark where you would put a bin, and say why you chose that place.
items.a: A street corner with a bin near where people wait or eat. A reason, such as people drop wrappers while they wait. The bin is clear of the drain.
items.why: People use a bin if it is close to where waste is made. A bin in a place where nobody passes does not help.

worksheets.title: Counts, paths and who cleans (stretch)
worksheets.context: This sheet stretches your thinking about numbers, the paths germs take, how a programme is judged and who does the cleaning.

items.p: A glass of clear water is tested and found to hold germs. What does that show?
opts: Clear water can still be unsafe to drink
Germs are always visible
All germs cause illness
items.why: Looking clean is not being clean. Many germs are too small to see, and some cause illness. Not all germs do, because most are harmless.

items.p: A forest floor covered in fallen leaves is dirty, because it is untidy.
items.why: False. The leaves feed the soil, and nothing harmful travels from them to a mouth. Untidy and unclean are different things.

items.p: A city makes 1.6 lakh tonnes of waste a day. Half is wet, which is ____ thousand tonnes.
items.why: 1.6 lakh is 160 thousand. Half of 160 thousand is 80 thousand tonnes.

items.p: Match each mix-up to what it spoils.
pairs: leftover food in a bag of paper
broken glass in a mixed bag
a battery in the wet bin
items.a: as given
items.why: Mixing waste moves a problem from one heap to all of them, and the next person pays for it.

items.p: Two heaps get the same peels. One is turned every week. One is packed tight. Which composts faster?
opts: The turned heap, because it gets more air
The packed heap, because it is warmer
Both take the same time
items.why: Bacteria and fungi that eat with air work faster. Turning lets air in. A packed heap runs short of air and turns sour.

items.p: A gobar gas plant also rots dung without air. Why is that useful there, and a problem in a dump?
items.a: In a closed tank, the methane is caught and burned for cooking. In a dump, the methane escapes, traps heat and can start fires.
items.why: The same airless rotting gives fuel when it is captured and harm when it is not. The difference is whether someone catches the gas.

items.p: Put these in order, first to last: a path from open faeces to an ill child.
a: Faeces is left in the open
A fly lands on the faeces
items.why: Each step hands the germs on. If you remove any step, such as a toilet at the start or a cover on the food, the chain breaks.

items.p: Soap blocks the path from fingers to mouth, and it does not block the path through unsafe water.
items.why: True. Soap works on the germs on hands. Safe water, a toilet and covered food block the other paths.

items.p: A flush toilet uses 10 litres a flush. A pour-flush pan uses 2 litres. How many litres do 5 pour-flushes save?
items.why: Each flush saves 10 − 2 = 8 litres. 8 × 5 = 40 litres.

items.p: Three of these are ways germs reach a mouth. Which one is the odd one out?
opts: Fingers
Flies
Rain washing into a well
A closed twin-pit toilet
items.why: A closed twin-pit toilet keeps the waste in a pit. Fingers, flies and well water are paths that carry germs.

items.p: A government counts toilets built, and researchers count toilets used. Why might the numbers differ?
opts: A toilet can exist and still not be used
One of the counts must be lying
Toilets vanish when counted
items.why: Both can be right. A toilet with no water, or with a pit the family fears to empty, may be built and not used.

items.p: Give one change the Swachh Bharat Mission made, and one thing people still argue about.
items.a: Changes: many more home toilets, and cleanliness became a talked-about subject. Arguments: whether the toilets are used, whether the numbers were counted fairly, and what happens to the waste.
items.why: A good answer gives one real change and one real argument.

items.p: Two views of a village that has declared itself open defecation free.

views.says: Every home has a toilet. We counted them one by one. The village is free.

views.who: A researcher who visits villages (an imagined view)
views.says: We asked who uses them and went at dawn. Some families still walk to the field.

items.ask: What would you want to know before deciding if the village is free?
items.a: Answers vary. A strong answer asks for both counts. It also asks why some families do not use their toilet, for example no water, a full pit or old habits.
items.why: Counting toilets is easy and counting use is harder. Both give true information, and only use tells you whether germs still reach the open.

items.p: Who cleaned your street or building today? Name two people and one other being, and say what each did.
items.a: A sweeper, a waste collector, a cleaner, and a crow, a cow, ants or bacteria. Each with the work they did, such as sweeping, lifting bags, eating scraps or breaking down peels.
items.why: Cleaning is done by many hands and by other beings. Noticing them is the first step to thanking them.

items.p: A shop stops giving thin bags. Which result shows that this works?
opts: Fewer bags found in drains and at clean-ups
More shops selling thin bags
More bags in the dry bin
items.why: A good test counts what we care about: bags that end up in drains and on the ground. Counting bags in a bin only shows where they went.

items.p: For one litter problem, draw a small action by a person and a bigger change by a city.
items.a: A child carrying a wrapper to a bin. A city adding bins and a daily collection. A company making packaging that can be recycled.
items.why: A clean place needs both. Small actions change habits, and bigger changes change what is easy.

worksheets.title: Faulty reasoning and open questions (challenge)
worksheets.context: This sheet asks you to spot faulty reasoning, weigh two views and think about questions that are still open.

items.p: Tipping dust outside the gate makes the whole neighbourhood cleaner.
items.why: False. The dust has only moved. A neighbour's house, a drain or a person's lungs now meets it.

items.p: A town's truck tips sorted wet and dry bags together into one pile. What is most likely?
opts: Mixing in the truck spoils both heaps
Nothing, because trucks sort by themselves
The dry waste becomes wet
items.why: Sorting at home only helps if the heaps stay apart. A mixed pile has the same problem as a mixed bin. The dry waste is made dirty and is no longer wet or dry.

items.p: A peel buried deep in a dump rots in the same way as in a compost pit.
items.why: False. In a pit with air, bacteria and fungi make compost. In a dump with no air, other bacteria make methane.

items.p: Methane is both a danger and a fuel. How can it be both?
items.a: It burns easily, so it can start fires in a dump and can run a stove when it is caught. It also traps heat in the air, which harms the climate when it escapes.
items.why: The same gas is harmful when it escapes and useful when it is captured, so what matters is whether anyone captures it.

items.p: India makes about 72,000 million litres of sewage a day. If one-third is treated, ____ million litres are not.
items.why: One-third of 72,000 is 24,000. 72,000 − 24,000 = 48,000 million litres. The real figure is less than a third treated, so the untreated amount is even larger.

items.p: Why does heavy rain make open defecation uphill of a well more dangerous?
opts: Rain washes germs along the ground into the well
Rain makes germs grow wings
Rain kills the germs
items.why: Water carries things downhill. A well downhill of a field can be spoilt by one heavy shower. Rain does not kill germs.

items.p: Sort each way of checking as a count of toilets built or toilets used.
items: a list of toilets in each village
asking each person where they went this morning
watching at dawn who walks to a field
counting concrete rings that were delivered
items.a: as given
items.why: A count of toilets built tells us about money and work. A count of use tells us about what people really do.

items.p: Match each cleaner to what they clear.
items.a: as given
items.why: People and other living beings do the cleaning, and each works on a different kind of waste.

items.p: Manual scavenging has been against the law since 1993, yet it still happens. What else is needed to end it?
items.a: Safe machines, so that nobody has to go down a sewer. Fair pay and safety gear for sanitation workers. Other jobs open to everyone. Respect, so that the work is no longer tied to birth.
items.why: A law says what must not happen. Ending it also needs machines, fair pay and an end to the idea that some people must do dirty work because of their birth.

items.p: Two views on cleaning toilets, from the early 1900s and 1940s.

views.says: Everyone should clean their own waste, because the work is noble. When all castes share it, no group is shamed.
Calling the work noble keeps it tied to one's birth. The work must be ended and replaced by other jobs for everyone.

items.ask: What would you do to make the work fair, and which view helps you most?
items.a: Answers vary. A strong answer gives a reason from one view, or uses both. For example, share cleaning in schools and homes, and also build machines and open other jobs.
items.why: Both men wanted to end the shame. Gandhi stressed sharing the work. Ambedkar stressed ending the link between work and birth.

items.p: A neighbour says: 'One wrapper makes no difference.' Which finding answers this?
opts: A littered place leads more people to litter
Wrappers rot in a day
Wind carries every wrapper away
items.why: Researchers found that people dropped more litter where there was already litter. One wrapper changes what the next person does.

items.p: Recycling is always better than reusing a thing as it is.
items.why: False. Recycling needs energy, water and work. Using a thing again as it is, or refusing it, avoids all of that.

items.p: Draw the path of a wrapper from a lane to the sea. Mark two places where it could be stopped.
items.a: Lane, then drain, then bigger drain, stream, river, sea. Stops marked, for example a bin at the lane, a grill or trap at the drain, a treatment plant before the river.
items.why: A wrapper follows the water. The earlier it is stopped, the fewer beings meet it.

items.p: Soil in a garden is soil. On a bed, it is dirt. Is 'dirty' in the thing or in the place?
items.a: Answers vary. A strong answer says that dirt is about where a thing is and what it can do there. Soil in a garden feeds plants. Soil on a bed gets onto skin and food. It may also say that germs are harmful in most places.
items.why: This is an open question. Scientists ask whether harmful things can travel to mouths, water and food. That depends on place and on the thing.

items.p: A family makes about 730 kilograms of waste a year, and half is wet. How many kilograms can be composted?
items.why: Half of 730 is 365 kilograms. If this is composted, that much stays out of the dump.

items.p: Two views on where to start, for a street that is covered in litter.

views.says: Start with children and families. A habit of carrying a wrapper to a bin lasts a lifetime.
Start with bins and a daily collection. People cannot use a bin that is not there.

items.ask: If you had a small budget, where would you start, and what evidence would you want?
items.a: Answers vary. A strong answer picks a start, gives a reason, and notes that the other view's part is also needed.
items.why: Habits and systems depend on each other. A good plan does both, and a good question is which comes first in your street.

spotted.text: Look at the bins in your building, school or market. Notice the colours. Green is for wet waste and blue is for dry waste. Look inside and see whether people really sort.
spotted.art: A row of a green bin and a blue bin outside an apartment gate, with a peel in the blue bin.

spotted.text: Watch the person who collects waste from your lane. Notice whether the truck or the cart has one space or two, and whether the sorted bags are tipped together at the back.
spotted.art: A collection auto in a lane with two compartments, one with green bags and one with blue bags.

spotted.text: Next time it rains, watch the drain in your lane for a minute. Notice what floats down and where the water goes. If a drain is blocked with bags, see where the water stands.
spotted.art: A rain-filled lane with a drain mouth and a few wrappers and a plastic bag drifting towards it.

spotted.text: At a tea stall, look at what the tea is served in. A clay kulhad, a paper cup and a plastic cup all end up on the ground sometimes. Notice which one is still there after the next rain.
spotted.art: Three used cups on the edge of a pavement, a clay kulhad, a paper cup and a plastic cup, after rain.

spotted.text: At a railway station or bus stand, look for red stains on walls and stairs, and for places where people wash hands. Notice whether there is soap beside the tap.
spotted.art: A station wall with red stains and a tap with no soap beside it.

spotted.text: At the vegetable market near closing time, see where the peels, stems and wilted leaves go. Notice if a cow, a crow, a heap or a truck gets them.
spotted.art: A vegetable seller's mat at dusk, a heap of stems and leaves, and a cow eating beside a broom.

spotted.text: Look at a packet of something you eat. Notice whether it says what to do with it, and whether it is one plastic or a shiny layer that is stuck together.
spotted.art: A hand holding a shiny chips packet with the shiny silver inside showing at the torn edge.

applications: Indore sends its sorted wet waste to a plant that makes gas for the city's buses. If your town collects wet waste separately, find out where it goes. Ask whether a plant, a compost yard or a dump is at the end.
Many housing societies in cities have a composter in the compound. Ask the person who looks after the garden how the peels become compost. Look at the heap and smell it.

Waste pickers in Pune work through their own cooperative, SWaCH. Pickers in Bengaluru carry city identity cards. If you see someone collecting sorted waste, look for the gloves, the apron or the card that shows the work is recognised.
Banana leaves and sal leaf plates are used at feasts and temples in South India and in the East. After the next feast, see where the leaves go, such as a cow, a compost pit or a heap.
A village twin-pit toilet uses about two mugs of water to flush. Compare that with a flush tank of ten litres. Find out how much water your own toilet uses by filling a bucket after one flush.
Hospitals and clinics keep used bandages and sharp things in sealed, coloured bags. Next time you see one, notice the colour and the sign that tells workers to be careful.
A steel tiffin, a cloth bag and a refilled bottle are used in thousands of homes in India. Count how many of these your family uses in a day, and how many thin bags and wrappers they replace.
ask_kids: Think of the last thing you threw away. Where is it right now, and who has touched it since?
If a place looks neat and has an open drain beside the hand pump, would you call it clean? Why?
Why does a heap of peels in a pot of soil turn into soil, and a heap in a plastic bag does not?
Who cleans the road you walk on to school? Have you ever said thank you to them?
Is it fair that people who make the least waste often do the most cleaning? What would be fair?
If nobody ever sees you drop a wrapper, is there still a reason not to? What is it?
A river cannot speak. If someone spoke for the river, what would they ask for?
What is one thing you could refuse this week, so that it never becomes waste?

jokes.j: What do you call a banana peel on its way to the compost pit?
jokes.a: A peel-grim on a long journey!

jokes.j: Why do crows make such good street sweepers?
jokes.a: They clean up everything, and then they caw about it.

jokes.j: Why was the soap so honest?
Knock knock. Who is there? Litter. Litter who?
jokes.a: Litter-ally everyone, if nobody picks me up!

jokes.j: Why did the vulture win the medal for the cleanest table?
jokes.a: She never left a single crumb.

jokes.j: Why did the earthworm love the compost heap?
jokes.a: It was an all-you-can-eat café, and the menu changed every day.

jokes.j: The cloth bag said to the thin carry bag, 'See you around.' What did the thin bag answer?
Why did the tippy-tap get so much attention?
jokes.a: It was always dripping with style.

jokes.j: Why did the dustbin go to the doctor?
jokes.a: It had too much on its plate, and everyone kept dumping on it.

maths.problem: In a dustbin count there were 20 wet items, 12 dry items and 3 harmful items. What fraction of all the items is wet? About what fraction is dry?
maths.answer: Wet: 20 out of 35, which is a little more than half. Dry: 12 out of 35, which is a little more than one-third.
maths.explain: Total = 20 + 12 + 3 = 35. Wet is 20 ÷ 35, a bit more than 17.5 ÷ 35 = half. Dry is 12 ÷ 35, a bit more than 11.67 ÷ 35 = one-third.
maths.context: This problem uses numbers like those from a one-day dustbin count to show each kind's share of the total.
maths.why_maths: A share is only meaningful against the total, so you must add all the heaps before you compare any one of them.

maths.problem: India's towns and cities make about 1.6 lakh tonnes of waste a day, or roughly half a kilogram for each person. About how many people is that? (1 tonne is 1,000 kilograms.)
maths.explain: 1.6 lakh tonnes = 160,000 × 1,000 = 160,000,000 kilograms. Divided by half a kilogram each: 160,000,000 ÷ 0.5 = 320,000,000, which is 32 crore.
maths.context: This problem uses the idea of a total and a share for each person to work backwards to a count of people.
maths.why_maths: Dividing a total by a share for each person tells you how many shares there are. It is the same sum that city planners use to plan trucks and bins.

maths.problem: A family of four makes about 2 kilograms of waste a day. How much waste does each person make in a year of 365 days?
maths.explain: 2 ÷ 4 = 0.5 kilograms for each person each day. 0.5 × 365 = 182.5 kilograms in a year.
maths.context: This problem shares a family's waste between its members and then scales it up to a year.
maths.why_maths: A rate for each person can be scaled to any number of days or people. This is how cities estimate waste for a whole population.

maths.problem: A tippy-tap uses 250 millilitres for one hand wash. A running tap uses about 1 litre. A bucket holds 10 litres. How many washes does the bucket give with each method?
maths.answer: With the tippy-tap, 40 washes. With the running tap, 10 washes.
maths.explain: 10 litres = 10,000 millilitres. 10,000 ÷ 250 = 40. 10,000 ÷ 1,000 = 10. The tippy-tap gives four times as many washes.
maths.context: This problem compares two ways of washing hands by how many washes one bucket of water gives.
maths.why_maths: Changing litres to millilitres lets you divide equal-sized units. This is how a village with one water tank decides how many people it can serve.

maths.problem: A family counted 24 wrappers and bottles on day 1 and 18 on day 7. By what fraction did the count fall? If it kept falling by the same amount each day, after how many more days would it reach zero?
maths.answer: It fell by one quarter. It fell by 6 in 6 days, which is 1 a day, so it would reach zero after 18 more days. It cannot really keep falling like that.
maths.explain: 24 − 18 = 6, and 6 out of 24 is one quarter. 6 fewer in 6 days is 1 fewer each day. 18 ÷ 1 = 18 more days. In real life, some waste always remains, so the pattern has to slow down.
maths.context: This problem uses a before-and-after count from a week of making less waste, and asks whether a pattern can go on for ever.
maths.why_maths: A pattern of change is a prediction, and an honest prediction asks where the pattern must stop.

warmup.q: What are the three kinds of waste that India's rules ask homes to keep apart?
Is a swept room always clean? Why or why not?
warmup.a: No. A room can look neat and still have germs or harmful waste that can reach people.

warmup.q: What does a peel become when bacteria and fungi eat the peel with air?
warmup.a: Compost, a dark, crumbly, soil-like material.

warmup.q: What gas forms when wet waste rots with no air?
warmup.a: Methane. It burns easily and traps heat.

warmup.q: Name two paths by which germs from faeces can reach a mouth.
warmup.a: Fingers, flies, fields, water or food. Any two.

warmup.q: Who sorts most of India's dry waste by hand?
Which comes first, recycling, reusing or refusing?
warmup.a: Refusing. If a thing is never made, nobody has to collect, sort or bury it.

warmup.q: What did people once believe caused cholera?
warmup.a: Bad smells. The cause was germs in water dirtied by faeces.

quiz: A place that looks neat is always clean.
A neat lane can have an open drain beside the hand pump.
Wet waste is waste that came from plants and animals and will rot.
Peels, tea leaves and leftover food are wet waste.
A peel buried in a dump with no air gives off methane.
Bacteria that live without air make methane as they eat.
Spit on a floor cannot hurt anyone, because it dries.
